q: A virtualised server farm is provisioned by ticket and billed annually. What can you conclude about its NIST characteristics?

items: **Rapid elasticity**: check whether resources scale rapidly
**Measured service**: check whether usage is metered
**Annual billing alone** does not prove that elasticity or measured service is absent

q: A CFO argues: 'Providers have economies of scale, so moving our steady 24/7 batch servers to the cloud must cut our bill.' Do you agree?

items: **Economies of scale** (standardised workloads, bulk hardware, stripped-down software) lower the **provider's** unit cost
**Steady 24/7 load** → gains little from **elasticity** or paying only when needed
**Compare total cost** and operational needs for this workload
a.foot: The case is stronger if load is **spiky** or the team wants to **stop running hardware**.

q: An internal platform lets departments create VMs from a portal in minutes and sends each department a monthly usage report, but it can only be reached from managed office desktops. Which NIST characteristic is in doubt, and which ones can't you judge yet?

items: **Look satisfied**: **self-service** and **measured service**
**In doubt: broad network access** → it expects access over the network through **standard mechanisms** from **varied clients**
**Internal-only is not the problem** → **private clouds** are valid
**Still unknown: resource pooling and rapid elasticity** → until you know whether capacity is shared and can grow and shrink quickly

q: A hosting firm rents fixed physical servers on 12-month contracts, reachable over the internet, and markets them as 'cloud'. Using the common thread of the cloud definitions, is the label justified?

items: **Internet access** gives only **network access**
**Common thread** of the definitions: **on-demand** provisioning from a **shared pool**, **rapidly provisioned and released** with **minimal provider interaction**
**Fixed servers on long contracts** → neither **elastic** nor **on demand**
a.foot: The label would hold if customers could **self-provision and release** capacity in minutes and **pay for what they use**.

q: A teammate says an internal private cloud is 'not real cloud' because one industry definition describes cloud as a service delivered to many external customers. How do you respond?

items: **Gartner**'s wording emphasises **multi-tenant** delivery to **external customers**
**NIST**, the anchor definition, is about **characteristics**, not who operates it

items.t: **A private cloud for one organisation is cloud** if it offers:

q: A startup expects anywhere between 1,000 and 200,000 users in its first year. Why does pay-as-you-go matter more to it than to a firm with flat, predictable load?

items: **Uncertain demand** → buying for peak means either a **large upfront investment** or **running out of capacity**
**Elasticity and usage-based spend** → cost follows actual users and makes **experiments cheap**
**Flat load** → the firm can size owned capacity accurately, so its gain from converting **CapEx to OpEx** is smaller
That gain has to be shown with a **total-cost comparison**

q: A bank and a fintech startup both want to launch a new payments feature on the cloud. Why will the bank's first-year plan look different?

sub: carries **regulatory, governance, security and privacy** obligations
**legacy systems** must be **migrated, integrated and co-exist** with the new feature

items: **Startup**: starts **cloud-first** on a **clean slate** → spends its effort on the product
**Bank's advantage**: existing **customers and data** → why integration is worth the cost

q: A team must apply a specific OS kernel patch and install custom middleware. Which service model fits, and what extra work comes with it?

a.lead: **IaaS**: the only model where the customer controls the **OS and middleware**.
items: **Extra work**: the team now **patches the OS**, **runs the middleware** and **configures scaling** itself
**If the kernel requirement went away** → **PaaS** would remove that work
a.foot: In return for PaaS you accept the provider's **supported languages and runtimes**.

q: An HR department needs leave management. A standard product covers 90% of its workflow, but there is one unusual approval rule. SaaS or an app built on PaaS?

a.lead: **SaaS** if the rule can be expressed through the product's **predefined settings**.
items: **SaaS** → gives the **least operational work**
**Build on PaaS** only if the rule is **essential** and **cannot be configured** → you write and **own the application** but avoid running servers
a.foot: Deciding factor: whether the **customisation is worth owning code for**.

q: Customer data leaks from a SaaS CRM because an employee shared a report with a public link. The team blames the provider. Who is accountable?

items: Even in **SaaS**, where the provider operates nearly every layer, **data classification**, **access decisions** and **accountability** stay with the customer
a.foot: Would differ if the leak came from a **breach of the provider's own infrastructure or application**, which are its layers.

q: A company runs its core system in its own data centre and its analytics on two public providers. A teammate calls this 'multi-cloud'. Is that the full description?

items: **Multi-cloud**: two public providers (mixing **vendors**)
**Hybrid**: connecting them to the **on-premises private** environment (mixing **cloud types**)

sub: hybrid → **integration and co-existence** concerns between environments

q: A team proposes a VPC to meet the rule 'customer data must not leave our premises'. Does it?

items: **VPC** = **logical network isolation** and **controlled access** inside the **provider's infrastructure** → data still sits on the **provider's premises**
**The rule calls for** a **private cloud**, or a **hybrid** design that keeps that data on premises
a.foot: A VPC fits when the requirement is **isolation with public-cloud scalability and pricing**, not **data location**.

q: A vendor offers a pre-integrated rack of hardware and cloud software to install in your data centre. Which deployment model is this, and how does it compare with building your own private cloud?

items: **What it is**: a complete **hardware plus software stack**, owned by the provider or sold for **on-premises** use
**vs your own private cloud**: **faster to stand up** than assembling one from parts
**But** you depend on that **vendor's stack** for upgrades and features
a.foot: You trade **build effort** for **lock-in**.

q: An exam answer for a web app's architecture says only 'use EC2, S3, RDS and CloudFront'. Why would it lose marks, and how should it be rewritten?

a.lead: It lists **product names** without the **need** each one meets or **why** it was chosen.
items: **Justify each choice** from the requirements
Major providers have **overlapping categories** → the **reasoning** carries the marks, not the product name

q: Two providers both cover compute, storage, databases, identity, ML and management tooling. Your client wants to pick one by comparing catalogue size. What should decide it instead?

items: **Decide from** the workload's **requirements** and the **cloud strategy**
**Finish the strategy before signing vendor contracts** (**Gartner** lists this as a common mistake)
**Keep an exit strategy**
**Favour containers and open standards** where **switching cost** matters

q: A team has 3 months to leave a data centre whose lease is ending. The application has stable load and no planned changes. Cloud-hosted or cloud-native?

items: **Minimal change** → the only way to meet the deadline
**Stable load** → gains little from **elasticity**
a.foot: Gives up the **resilience, autoscaling and automation** gains of a redesign, but selected components can be made **cloud-optimised** later, once the deadline is met.

q: The CEO announces: 'We are cloud-first. Every system moves next year, starting with our ERP.' Critique this as a strategy.

a.lead: It makes several of **Gartner's mistakes** at once:
items: **Executive mandate** treated as a strategy
**Cloud-first** read as **cloud-only**
**Starting with a critical, complex workload** like ERP

q: A security officer says: 'Cloud is less secure, so mission-critical systems must stay on premises.' Do you agree?

items: **'Less secure'** and **'not for mission-critical'** are both listed **cloud myths**
**Security depends on design** and on the **responsibility split**
**Provider** secures its layers; the **customer** must still secure its own **configuration, identities and data**
a.foot: A specific **regulatory or data-location constraint**, not the myth, is the valid reason to keep a system on premises.

q: A team builds heavily on one provider's proprietary queue and database APIs to go cloud-native quickly. What risk are they taking, and how could they limit it?

a.lead: **Risk**: deep use of proprietary services raises **switching cost** and reduces **portability**.
items: **Limit it**: **containers and open standards** where they matter
**Isolate provider-specific calls** behind their own interfaces
**Keep an exit strategy**
a.foot: Trade-off: avoiding **managed proprietary services** gives up some of the **speed** that made cloud-native attractive.

q: A retailer runs a 6-week seasonal web shop. Evening traffic is 20 times the daytime level, the team is two developers, and there is no ops staff. Recommend a service model and a deployment model, and say what would make you choose IaaS instead.

a.lead: **PaaS on a public cloud**, with **SaaS** for commodity parts such as **payments or email**.
items: **PaaS** → the provider runs the **OS and runtime**
**Elasticity** → absorbs the **evening peaks** without the retailer owning peak capacity
**Spend follows the 6-week season** instead of a **year-round investment**
a.foot: **Choose IaaS** only if the shop needs **OS-level control** or **middleware** the platform doesn't support, and accept that the **two developers** would then **patch and scale servers** themselves.

q: A regulated bank must keep customer records in its own data centre but wants elastic capacity for a new customer-facing app. Recommend a deployment model, and explain why a VPC alone is not enough.

items: **Customer records** stay in the **on-premises private environment**
**Elastic front end** runs on **public cloud**
Connected through **controlled integration**
**VPC alone is not enough** → **logical isolation** inside the **provider's infrastructure**, but does not keep data on the **bank's premises**
a.foot: Costs: **governance, integration and co-existence** work across two environments, plus the **latency** of calls back to on-premises data.

q: An enterprise wants its first cloud project to be moving its 15-year-old, heavily customised ERP. Advise on whether it should go first, and compare IaaS, PaaS and SaaS for it when it does move.

sub: **Gartner** warns against starting with **critical, complex, large** workloads like ERP
**IaaS** (**cloud-hosted lift and shift**): keeps the **customisation**, needs the **least change**, but keeps all the **OS and middleware** work
**SaaS**: removes most of the **operations** but forces the business onto **predefined settings** → may mean dropping **years of customisation**

q: A proposal says: 'Move to the cloud to save money, and use two providers so disaster recovery is automatic.' Evaluate both claims and say what evidence you would want.

items: **Cloud is not always cheaper**
**Multi-cloud** does not by itself **save money** or **improve DR** → it adds **cross-provider skills and operations**
a.foot: Multi-cloud may still be justified for **specific reasons**, but it should come with an **exit strategy** rather than an assumed benefit.

q: An IT department rebrands its virtualisation cluster as 'our private cloud'. Developers can create VMs from a portal in minutes, but capacity is fixed at 200 VMs, adding hosts takes a 6-week purchase, and there is no usage reporting. Assess the claim against NIST and recommend what would close the gaps.

items: **On-demand self-service**: met by the **portal**
**Resource pooling**: a **shared cluster** suggests it
**Rapid elasticity**: fails → the **200-VM cap** and **6-week purchase** stop capacity from growing quickly
**Measured service**: fails → nothing is **metered**
**Virtualisation alone is not a private cloud**

sub: either keep **spare capacity** or **burst to public cloud** (a **hybrid** model) so capacity can grow on demand

q: A company is about to move 40 applications to the cloud and asks whether its existing solution architects can simply take this on. What gap would a cloud architect fill?

items: **Solution architect**: designs a solution for a **given set of requirements**

items.t: **Cloud architect**: owns the **cloud strategy** across them
sub: oversight of **cloud management and governance policies**

items: **Without that role** → **40 separate solution designs** would each make their own cloud choices
a.foot: A **small estate** could combine the roles, but the **strategy and governance** work still has to be owned by someone.

q: Users complain that a reporting portal's data is correct but hard to find and interpret, while the DBA says the schema is well normalised. Which architect role should look at this, and why not the other?

items: **Information architect**: focuses on how users **experience and interact with data**
**Data architect**: designs and manages **data structures**, and the schema is already sound
**The problem** is **presentation and navigation** rather than **storage**

q: An enterprise with 200 on-premises VMs and a board deadline wants to start its cloud adoption with lift and shift to IaaS. Is that a sound first step, and what should it not assume?

items: **Changes little**
Moves infrastructure spend to a **usage-based operating model** quickly
**Don't assume lower or predictable total spend** → predictable **unit prices** still depend on **sizing and usage**
A **lifted app** gains little **elasticity**
a.foot: Plan which applications to **redesign later**.

q: Two new projects arrive: an IoT telemetry service with unpredictable device growth, and an internal timesheet tool used by 50 staff. Which should be cloud-native and which can simply be cloud-enabled?

sub: needs **automatic scaling** under load or failure

items: **Timesheet tool → cloud-enabled**: **small, steady load**, so moving it **as is** is enough
a.foot: Native design is only worth its cost where **elasticity, statelessness and automation** actually pay off.

q: A teammate says 'it isn't cloud-native unless it runs on Kubernetes with microservices.' Do you agree?

items: **Orchestrated containers and microservices** are common ways to build cloud-native apps
**Defining idea**: design for **cloud properties** such as **elasticity, automation and easy integration**
A **serverless app** or a **well-designed monolith** that **scales and recovers automatically** can also qualify

q: A team has containers running under a container runtime on three VMs and says they are ready for production. What is missing?

sub: **orchestration** for deployment, scaling and failure recovery

items: **If the services need them**: **persistent storage** and **messaging**
**Without orchestration** → a crashed container or failed VM needs **manual recovery**

q: A platform has 6 services behind an API gateway. The team wants a service mesh as well. Would you add it now?

items: **API gateway** → already handles external **north-south** traffic
**Service mesh** → manages internal **east-west** traffic (**load balancing, encryption, retries**); pays off when many services need **uniform inter-service policy**
**With 6 services** → **library-level retries and TLS** may be enough
a.foot: Revisit when the **service count** or the need for **mutual TLS** and **traffic policy** grows.

q: Orders must reach billing, shipping and analytics, and billing is sometimes down for maintenance. Synchronous HTTP API calls or event streaming and messaging?

items: The order service **publishes once**
Each consumer processes **at its own pace**
**Billing catches up** after maintenance instead of **failing the order**
**Cost**: **eventual consistency** and an **extra platform** to operate
a.foot: Keep a **synchronous API** where the caller needs an **immediate answer**, such as a **price check**.

q: A legacy app costs a lot to run on lifted VMs because it can't scale down at night. Would you do a complete refactor, a partial refactor or stay lifted?

a.lead: **Partial refactor** is the usual first answer.
items: **Target the component that blocks scale-down** → e.g. extract the **stateless web tier** so it can **autoscale**
**Complete refactor**: only if **measured long-term gains** outweigh its higher **cost, time and risk**
**Stay lifted**: fine if the **night-time waste** is smaller than the **refactoring cost**

q: After a regional outage, the team rebuilds its whole network and cluster from IaC in another region in 20 minutes, but the app still won't start. What was most likely missing from the DR plan?

items: **Missing**: the **data, secrets and configuration** the app needs were probably not **restored or replicated** to the recovery region

sub: a way to restore **secrets and config** alongside the IaC

q: Engineers fix production servers by hand during incidents, and test now behaves differently from production. How does IaC address this, and what discipline does it require?

items: **Environments in versioned, reviewed code** with **deliberate parameter differences**
→ **consistent dev, test and prod**
→ removes **untracked manual changes**
**Discipline**: **every change**, including **incident fixes**, goes through the **code and the pipeline**
a.foot: Otherwise **drift** returns, and the **next apply** may **overwrite the hand fix**.

q: A scan finds a shell and package manager in a production image that runs as root and is patched in place. Which image practices does this break, and what would you change?

sub: rebuild from a **verified minimal or distroless base**
**replace containers** with a new patched image instead of **patching them in place**

items: **Gain** → shrinks the **attack surface** and limits what an attacker can do **after a compromise**
a.foot: Cost: harder **interactive debugging**.

q: A firm containerised every app and runs them on Kubernetes in two clouds, and now says it can 'move any workload between clouds in an hour'. What has it overlooked?

items: **Containers and Kubernetes definitions** standardise **packaging and orchestration** (**multi-cloud 2.0**)
**Do not move with the image**: **data**, **IAM policies**, **networking** and dependencies on **proprietary managed services**
A workload using one provider's **managed database** still needs its **data migrated** and its **integration rewritten**
a.foot: The claim holds only for **stateless apps** with **portable dependencies**.

q: A company uses a broker to place its HR system on one cloud and its analytics on another, and each app stays in its own cloud. Which multi-cloud generation is this, and what does it fail to give?

items: Workloads are **spread across clouds**, but each app is **tied to one provider**
**Fails to give**: **workload portability** → moving an app means **migrating** it
**Multi-cloud 2.0**: **containerises** workloads so they can be **recreated elsewhere**
a.foot: Multi-cloud 2.0 costs running **Kubernetes consistently** in each cloud.

q: You must design a cloud platform for a new government agency. Should you start from a vendor's reference architecture or a neutral one such as NIST 500-292?

a.lead: Use a **neutral** one to frame the **actors and building blocks**, then a **vendor's** reference architecture once the provider is chosen.
items: **Neutral (NIST 500-292 or CCRA)** → keeps the design **vendor-neutral** and helps the agency **compare options**
**Vendor reference architectures** → concrete starting points with **proven component combinations**
a.foot: But vendor ones **lean toward that vendor's services**.

q: An online game's player count jumps 10 times during weekend events, and a zone outage last month took it offline. What two design features address these problems, and what does each cost?

items.t: **Auto-scaled web and app tiers** → absorb the **event spikes**
sub: **Cost**: needs **stateless servers**, with **sessions** moved to an **in-memory cache**

items.t: **Two Availability Zones** behind a **load balancer** → keeps the game up if one **zone fails**

q: The DR design uses a synchronous standby in a second AZ and snapshots copied to another region. A manager asks why both are needed. Explain, including what each one loses.

sub: **Loses**: does nothing if the **whole region** fails
**Loses**: recover only to the **last copied snapshot**
need **time to restore** a new instance

a.foot: Choose **snapshot frequency** against acceptable **data loss**, and **restore capacity** against acceptable **downtime**.

q: An e-commerce team must choose between a classic stack (load-balanced, auto-scaled app servers with a shared relational database) and a serverless design with Product, Payment, Inventory and Cart functions behind an API gateway, each with its own store. Traffic is low most of the year with sharp sale peaks. Which fits, and what do you give up?

items: **Functions scale** with the **sale peaks** and **cost little** in quiet months
**Separate stores** → each service **scales and changes independently**
**Give up**: simple **cross-service transactions and joins** → **inventory and payment consistency** now needs **coordination**
**Accept**: **function limits** and **cold starts**
a.foot: A **steady, high base load** would favour the **classic stack**.

q: A company runs a 10-year-old monolith on premises. The data-centre contract ends in 6 months, and the checkout module struggles at month-end peaks. Recommend a migration approach, and say what would justify a complete refactor.

a.lead: **Lift and shift to IaaS first**, then **partially refactor** the checkout module.
items: **Lift and shift** → meets the **6-month deadline** with **minimal change**
**Partial refactor** → e.g. extract checkout as a **stateless, autoscaled service**
**Leave the rest** of the monolith alone until **measured benefits** justify more work
**Complete refactor**: justified only if **long-term performance and operating-cost gains** outweigh its higher **cost, time and risk**
a.foot: Note: the **lifted monolith** may **cost more to run** than expected until it is **optimised**.

q: A platform team manages dev, test and prod by hand, and an outage last quarter took 3 days to recover. Justify Infrastructure as Code, explain how you would keep the environments consistent but deliberately different, and say what IaC will not solve.

items: **Shared, versioned IaC modules** with **explicit per-environment parameters** (**sizes, replica counts**) and **separate state**
**Changes go through Git review** and are **applied automatically** → reduces **drift** and **documents** the environment
**Rebuild** then takes **minutes instead of days**
**IaC will not restore** **data, secrets or application configuration** → DR also needs **backups or replication** and a **tested recovery runbook**

q: A regulated insurer must keep policyholder data on premises, wants elastic capacity for quote calculations, and its CTO also wants a second public cloud 'to avoid lock-in'. Design the strategy and judge the second cloud.

items: **Policyholder data** stays in the **private environment**
**Stateless quote calculation** on **public cloud**, sending **only the data it needs** over a **secured link**
**Second public cloud** only for a **concrete reason**, such as a **lock-in risk** or a **best-of-breed service**
**Containerising on Kubernetes** → workloads **portable** (**multi-cloud 2.0**), but **data, identity and managed-service dependencies** still tie them to a provider
a.foot: Every added environment increases **integration, skills and management cost**.

q: A startup runs 12 containerised microservices and has had two outages: one from a bad manual deployment and one from a retry storm between services. What components would you add to make the platform production-ready, and which outage does each address?

sub: either a **service mesh** or **consistent client libraries** for **retry limits, timeouts and circuit breaking**
at **12 services** a mesh is **defensible** but adds **operating cost**

q: Design the architecture for an online game with spiky weekend traffic, global players downloading large assets, real-time leaderboards, and a target of surviving a full region outage. Explain each component's purpose.

items: **Auto-scaled web and app tiers** across **two AZs** behind a **load balancer** → handle the **spikes** and **zone failure**
**In-memory cache** → holds **sessions and leaderboards** so servers stay **stateless** and **reads are fast**
**Object storage and a CDN** → serve **large assets** close to players
**Replicated database** with a **synchronous standby** → covers **zone failure**
**Region outage** → **copy snapshots to a second region** and **restore them with automation**
a.foot: Accept **data loss back to the last snapshot** and a **restore delay**.

q: A change that passed in test fails in production, and the team finds production was hand-edited months ago. How would IaC have prevented this, and does it mean test must be identical to production?

sub: the **same reviewed modules** build every environment and **all changes go through code** → the hand edit could not have **drifted unnoticed**
**size, access and region** should be **explicit parameters**

a.foot: Drift only stays away if **nobody makes manual changes** outside the code.

q: VMs and databases are created correctly from templates, but an app fails because a library version on the VMs differs from the one expected. Which IaC component is missing, and which would not help?

items: **Configuration management**: makes sure the **software** on provisioned resources is **set up as intended**
**Would not help**: **provisioning** (only created the resources correctly) and **orchestration** (manages **deployment workflows and scaling**) → neither addresses **what is installed on the VMs**
**Another way**: bake the dependency into an **immutable image**

q: Three product teams each copy and edit the same 800-line network template, and a security fix had to be made in three places. Which IaC best practices would you apply?

items: **Modular design**: extract a **reusable, versioned networking module** that every team consumes with **its own parameters** → a fix is **made once and rolled out**
**Environment segmentation**: **Dev, Test and Prod** are **isolated**
**State management**: each apply knows the **current infrastructure**
a.foot: Trade-off: changes to a **shared module** need **versioning and testing**, because one change now affects **every team**.

q: Two engineers run applies against the same environment at the same time and resources end up duplicated. Which best practice was missing, and why does it matter?

items: The tooling needs **one tracked record** of the **current infrastructure**, kept in **one shared place** that **every apply reads and updates**
**Without it** → each apply works from a **different view of reality**
→ **updates or scaling** create **duplicates** or **destroy resources unexpectedly**

q: In one project, the function, API and table are defined in the IaC template, but permissions and logging are configured by hand in the console afterwards. What is the risk?

a.lead: **Security and observability settings are not versioned.**
items: → a **redeploy** or a **new environment** can come up **without them**, or with **different permissions**
**Lecture's serverless template**: defines **permissions and logging** alongside the resources → they **deploy the same way every time**
a.foot: Cost: a **larger template** that must be **reviewed carefully**.

q: A containerised app reaches its database over a public endpoint protected by IP firewall rules. A reviewer asks for private endpoints in the virtual network and a role assignment for the cluster instead. What does each change gain, and what does it cost?

items.t: **Private endpoint** → database traffic stays on the **private network**
sub: the database is **not exposed to the internet** at all
**firewall rules** on a public endpoint can be **misconfigured** or **bypassed** by a **compromised allowed address**
**no secret** has to be **stored and rotated**

a.foot: Costs: more **network design** and harder access for **tools outside the network**.

q: A company is all-in on one cloud and is choosing between that provider's native declarative IaC and Terraform. What should decide it?

items: **Everything on one provider** → **native tools** are **designed for its services** and **model them directly** → favours them
**Terraform** → if the company expects to **span clouds** or wants **one language and workflow** across providers
a.foot: Trade-off: **depth on one cloud** versus **portability of skills and tooling**.

q: One Terraform configuration creates clusters on three providers. A manager says 'we now have one cross-cloud cluster'. Is that right?

a.lead: **No.** It provisions **separate clusters** with a **common tool and workflow**.
items: **GitOps** can keep **workload definitions in sync**
a.foot: A common tool reduces the **provisioning work** but does not make the clusters **one system**.

q: An operator scales a Deployment by hand with a command during an incident. Ten minutes later it is back to its old size. Why, and what should they have done?

items: **Why**: under **GitOps** the **declared state in Git** is the **source of truth** → the **sync tool reconciled** the live cluster back to it

sub: make the change as a **reviewed Git commit**
or **pause reconciliation deliberately** during the incident, with the **fix committed afterwards**

a.foot: This is the **declarative model** working as intended: **imperative changes do not last**.

q: A bad release is reverted in Git and the cluster syncs, but the app still fails. What does a Git rollback not undo?

items: **Reverting a commit** restores the **desired configuration**
**Does not undo**: **persistent data** or a **database schema migration** the new version already applied
**Old version can't read the new schema** → the **rollback fails**

sub: **backward-compatible schema changes** or a **data recovery step**
check that the cluster has actually **converged** before declaring recovery

q: In an event-driven pipeline, every component is provisioned with a single broad service identity because it was quicker. What would you change in the IaC, and why there?

items: **Own identity per component** with **only the permissions it needs** → e.g. **publish-only** for the producer, **write-only to the analytics table** for the processor
**Why in IaC** → applies the **least-privilege** policy **the same way every time** and keeps it **under review**
a.foot: Cost: **more identities and policies** to manage, but a **compromised component** can no longer **reach everything**.

q: A company's Dev, Test and Prod environments keep drifting apart, two engineers sometimes apply changes at the same time, and 30% of production deployments fail. Propose an IaC-based remedy and say what discipline it requires from the team.

items: **Reusable, versioned modules in Git** for all infrastructure
**Environment segmentation**: each environment is a **separate, isolated set of parameters**
**One shared, tracked state** → **concurrent applies** work from the **same view**
**Apply only through a pipeline** after **review**
**Configuration management or immutable images** → keep the **software consistent** too
a.foot: Discipline: it only works if **nobody changes infrastructure by hand**; **incident fixes** must also go through code.

q: Choose IaC tooling for (a) a 5-person startup building only on one provider's serverless services and (b) an enterprise running Kubernetes on three providers. Justify each, and say what each choice gives up.

sub: can define **functions, APIs, tables, permissions and logging** in **one template**
**Gives up**: **portability** if the startup later **spans clouds**

items.t: **(b) Enterprise**: **Terraform** with a **provider per cloud** and **reusable cluster modules**, plus **GitOps** for the workloads
sub: **Gives up**: some **native depth**; **connectivity** and **federated identity** still have to be designed separately

q: Design the IaC for an event-driven pipeline: messages are ingested, processed by functions and written to an analytics store. A security review requires that a compromised processor cannot read or delete other data. Explain the security decisions in the template.

items: **One declarative configuration** provisions the **topic, subscription, function and analytics tables**, with **monitoring and logging** defined alongside
**Own identity per component** → the **processor** can only **consume from its subscription** and **write to its table**
**Permissions defined in IaC** → **reviewed** and **applied the same way** in **every environment**
a.foot: Trade-off: **more identities** to manage, in exchange for a **much smaller blast radius**.

q: A team uses GitOps for its Kubernetes platform. A release that adds a database column fails, and an engineer proposes 'just revert the commit'. Explain what GitOps gives here and what the revert will and will not fix.

items: **What GitOps gives**: **declared state in Git** + **automation reconciles** the cluster to it → **traceability**, **review** and a **quick way back** to the previous configuration
**Revert will fix**: restores the **old Deployment**
**Revert will not fix**: the **schema change** has already been applied → if the old version can't work with the **new column**, the app **still fails**
**Instead**: **backward-compatible migrations** or a **data recovery step**, and **verify convergence** before calling it fixed

q: A reviewer compares two IaC designs for a containerised app and its database. Design A exposes the database on a public endpoint with IP allow-lists and stores a database password in the cluster. Design B places the database behind a private endpoint in the virtual network, puts a web application firewall at the edge, and grants the cluster a role assignment. Which would you approve, and what does B cost?

items: **Private endpoint** → removes **public exposure** of the database
**WAF** → filters **malicious traffic** at the **edge**
**Identity-based role assignment** → removes a **long-lived secret** that could leak
**All defined in the template** → the **same controls** present in **every environment**
a.foot: B costs more **network design**, and **tools outside the network** can't reach the database without a **controlled path**.

q: A team moved from VMs to containers to cut scale-out time, but new replicas still take 90 seconds to serve traffic. What is the likely cause, and what would you check?

items: **Containers skip booting a guest OS** because they **share the host kernel**
**Likely cause**: **pulling a large image**, **loading dependencies** and **initialising the application** can still **dominate startup**
**Check**: **image size** and **pull time**, and how long the application takes to **warm up**
a.foot: **Smaller images** and **lighter initialisation** help more than changing the **isolation boundary**.

q: A legacy app needs a Windows kernel feature, and a second workload from a different tenant must run on the same hosts with strong separation. VMs or containers for each?

items: **Legacy app** needs **its own OS** → a container **sharing the host kernel** cannot provide it
**Hypervisor boundary** → **stronger separation between tenants** than **process-level isolation**
a.foot: You give up the **lighter weight** and **faster startup** of containers, which matter less for these two requirements.

q: A company with a 3-person IT team wants to migrate to the cloud this year but has no cloud skills. Should it run the migration itself or use a managed cloud service, and what is the catch?

items: A provider takes on **migration, configuration, optimisation, security and maintenance**, usually on **subscription**
→ the **small team** gets cloud benefits without **building every skill first**
**Catch**: the **ongoing subscription cost** and **dependence on the provider**
The **contract** must be in place **before migrating**
a.foot: The company still **owns its data and decisions**.

q: A university wants a private IaaS cloud on its own hardware and asks what a hypervisor alone would be missing. Using OpenStack's components, explain.

a.lead: A **hypervisor runs VMs**, but an **IaaS cloud** needs more.

items.t: **OpenStack** supplies these on top of **compute (Nova)**, for example:

items: **Without them** → users still depend on **administrators** to wire each VM together → fails **on-demand self-service**

q: A security team won't allow extra agents on production servers but wants the servers' configuration managed as code. Does Ansible fit, and what does it still need?

items: **No resident agent** has to be installed on each target

sub: whatever **prerequisites its modules require** on the target

a.foot: The security team's concern then shifts to protecting those **credentials** and the **control node**.

q: An engineer calls an Ansible playbook a Heat template 'because both are YAML' and wants to feed the playbook to Heat. What is wrong?

items: **Ansible** runs a **playbook's ordered tasks**
**Heat** interprets **HOT templates** to **orchestrate OpenStack resources**
Each tool needs **its own format**
a.foot: Either can describe **infrastructure as code**: choose by whether you need **OpenStack-native orchestration** or **general provisioning and configuration** across systems.

q: A team's API uses a managed database, a queue and CI/CD, and needs no OS changes. A second system is a backup server that needs custom storage drivers. Which fits PaaS and which IaaS?

items: **API → PaaS**: consumes **managed platform services**; the platform takes over **deployment, scaling and runtime management**
**Backup server → IaaS**: needs **server-level control** of **drivers and storage**
a.foot: With PaaS the team still **configures access** and **secures its own code**.

q: A vendor pitch says moving to PaaS will 'cut delivery time from months to hours'. How would you treat this claim in a business case?

a.lead: As an **illustrative benefit**, not a **guaranteed saving**.
items: **PaaS removes server setup** and **platform operations** → can shorten delivery a great deal
**Real gain** depends on how much of the current delay is **infrastructure work** rather than **design, testing or approvals**
**Measure** the **current lead time** and its **causes** before promising a figure

q: A multi-tenant SaaS platform plans to run every customer's code in containers on shared hosts. A security reviewer objects. What is the concern, and what are the options?

items: **Concern**: containers isolate processes through **kernel namespaces and cgroups** but **share the host kernel** → a **kernel exploit** can reach **other tenants**
**VMs** isolate at the **hardware level** through a **hypervisor** and come with **established security tooling**

sub: **containers grouped onto VMs by tenant** → keeps most of the containers' **speed**

q: A firm must leave its data centre in 4 months and its apps are over-provisioned. Lift-and-shift or lift-and-optimise?

items: The **deadline** and **low initial change** matter most
It **carries the over-provisioning** into the cloud → budget for **right-sizing and optimisation after cutover**
**Lift-and-optimise** → lower **ongoing TCO** and **improves ROI sooner**, but **takes longer** and **costs more up front**
a.foot: The **4-month window** doesn't allow lift-and-optimise.

q: A business owner says 'our app is too expensive, let's rewrite it as microservices'. Using the six drivers, what would you check before agreeing?

items: **Driver is cost** (infrastructure too expensive for the value) → **Rehost** or **Replatform** may fix it far more cheaply
**Rewrite justified** when the drivers are **business fit, innovation or agility** → the app can't **meet needs** or **change fast enough**
**Cause-effect analysis** → shows whether the problem is **functional, architectural or technological**
The option should **fix that cause**

q: The migration roadmap lists 'do not move' and 'decommission' as paths alongside lift-and-shift and refactor. Why is it worth assessing every application before picking a default path?

items: Some apps are better **left in place** or **switched off** → moving them **wastes effort** and adds **cloud cost**
**Discover and assess** each app first, then **plan and sequence by dependency**
→ avoids **migrating something only to retire it later**
a.foot: Cost: the time spent on **discovery** before anything moves.

q: A bank wants its transaction system on a managed cloud database but cannot touch the business logic. Rehost or Replatform?

items: **Swaps the platform** (the database) with **minimal compatibility changes**; **code structure and features** stay the same
**Rehost** would move the app with its existing **self-managed database unchanged**
a.foot: Replatform adds **testing for database compatibility** in exchange for **less database operations work**.

q: After a Rehost, the business asks why the app's features and slow reports didn't improve. Is the migration a failure?

items: **Rehost changes only where the app runs** → its benefits are **infrastructure** ones
**Faster reports or new features** → need **Replatform** (e.g. a **managed analytics service**) or deeper options
a.foot: Set those **expectations in the business case**.

q: A retailer's app runs fine but the database can't cope with holiday peaks, and the code must not change. What option fits, and what would push you further along the spectrum?

items: Addresses the **peaks** without touching **code structure**
**What pushes further**: the **code itself blocks scaling** (e.g. **shared state in the app tier**) → Replatform won't be enough → **Rearchitect**
a.foot: Rearchitect comes at **higher cost and risk**.

q: An app's features are fine, but one module can't scale and every change is risky because of technical debt. A teammate proposes Rebuild. Do you agree?

a.lead: **Rearchitect** is the better fit, not Rebuild.
items: **Rearchitect**: restructures the existing code **without changing external behaviour** → e.g. **extract the bottleneck module** so it **scales independently**
It reduces **technical debt**
**Rebuild**: **rewrites everything**, carries the **highest cost and risk**
a.foot: Rebuild is justified only when **new capabilities** such as **mobile-first, IoT or AI** are needed.

q: A mainframe holds valuable pricing logic that a new mobile app needs, but the mainframe is too risky to change this year. Retain, Encapsulate or Rebuild?

items: Expose the **pricing data and functions as APIs** → the mobile app uses them **without rewriting the internals**
**Plain Retain** → leaves the logic **inaccessible** to the new app
**Rebuild** → the **risk** the business wants to avoid
a.foot: Cost: the **legacy system stays in place**, and its **performance and availability** now **limit the new app**.

q: A department's expense tool is home-grown, offers nothing unique, and its developer has left. Which option fits, and what goes with it?

a.lead: **Replace** with a **COTS or SaaS** product, and **Retire** the old tool as part of the move.
items: Take **current requirements** into account
**Not a differentiator** → **owning code adds no value**
a.foot: Cost: **users adapt** to the product's **workflow**, and **data has to be migrated** before **decommissioning**.

q: Rebuild scores highest on value in Gartner's comparison. Why is it not the default answer?

items: Rebuild also has the **highest cost of change**, the **highest risk** and a **long time to value**
**Diagnosed drivers only call for infrastructure or platform fixes** → **Rehost** or **Replatform** give **faster, cheaper, lower-risk** results
**Choose the lightest option** that **fixes the drivers**
a.foot: Keep **Rebuild** for when **business logic or UX must change**.

q: Leadership wants the first cloud migration to be the system with the biggest projected ROI, a customer-facing billing platform. How do you respond?

items: **Seven-step plan**: **start simple** and **prioritise learning over ROI**
**First project** should be **low-risk** and **highly instructive** → **early success** builds **skills and buy-in**
**Billing platform** is **strategically important** and **high-risk** → a failure would **set back the whole programme**
a.foot: Migrate it in a **later wave**, once the **landing zone** and **operating model** have been proven.

q: Two candidate first workloads score the same on architecture, security, availability and performance. One team is eager, the other was told to migrate. Which would you pick?

items: **Team enthusiasm** is one of the **eight classification criteria** → migrations need the **owning team's engagement**
**A willing team** → an **early success** and **useful lessons** more likely
The other workload can follow once there is a **proven pattern to copy**

q: Six months into migration, a CFO sees costs higher than before and wants to stop. What is the likely explanation, and what would you show?

items: **Costs rise temporarily**: **duplicate environments, training, consultants, tools and lease penalties**
→ until **old infrastructure is retired** and **optimisation** starts
**Show**: **lifetime TCO** against the **baseline**, and the **dates when on-premises costs stop**
a.foot: The CFO's concern is valid if the **business case never showed savings**, or **retirement keeps slipping**.

q: An app processes citizens' health records and must stay within national borders. The preferred provider has no local region. How does this assessment concern affect the plan?

a.lead: **Jurisdiction and regulation** can **rule out regions or providers** → that provider is **excluded** for this app, no matter what else it offers.

sub: a **private or hybrid placement** for the records

items: **Encryption and privacy controls** are still needed, but they **don't remove** a **data-location rule**

q: A portfolio analysis assigns Rehost to an app with 2 years of remaining life and high audit risk. Which assessment concerns would make you question that choice?

items: **2 years left** → **Retain** or **Retire** may cost less than migrating
**Audit risk** → check **compliance in the target environment** before moving
The **planning framework** expects each app's **R** to come from these **concerns**, not from a **default**

q: A company's CRM is not a differentiator, has simple processes, and needs specialist skills it cannot hire. What sourcing and hosting model would you suggest?

a.lead: **Partner** sourcing, most likely **SaaS** hosting → effectively a **Replace** decision.
items: **All three sourcing factors** point to a **partner**
**Gives up**: **deep customisation** and **control of the roadmap**
a.foot: Acceptable for a **non-differentiating** capability.

q: A trading firm's pricing engine is its main differentiator and has complex logic, but it needs rare low-latency skills. The sourcing factors conflict. How do you decide?

items: **Differentiation carries the most weight** (**60%** in the example) → outweighs **skills** pointing to a **partner**
**Skills gap** → **hiring or training**, or use a **partner** only for **specialised infrastructure work**
a.foot: **Validate with stakeholders**: the weights are a **decision aid**, not a rule.

q: Using the example weights, a capability scores differentiation 3, complexity 2 and skills 1. What does the result suggest, and what should you do with it?

items: **Result** → leans toward **internal sourcing** in the example
**Skills is scored inversely** → the **1** means **highly specialised skills** are needed → a real **gap to plan for**
**Validate** against **actual skills and constraints**, and test risky choices with a **proof of concept**

q: A hospital's 15-year-old on-premises patient scheduling system slows down at morning peaks. The code is stable and meets business needs, but the database server is end-of-life, and patient data must stay in the country. Recommend a migration option, justify it with the drivers, and name two risks to manage.

a.lead: **Replatform**: move to a **managed database** and **auto-scaling** in an **in-country region**, with **minimal code change**.
items: **Drivers**: **risk** (**end-of-life platform**) and **scalability**, not **business fit**
**Not Rebuild** → would add **cost and risk** without fixing anything the business needs

sub: **database compatibility** → test on the new engine, ideally with a **proof of concept**

a.foot: Budget for the **migration bubble** while **both environments run**.

q: A firm must exit its data centre in 6 months, with 80 apps, many over-provisioned. The CFO expects savings in year one. Compare lift-and-shift and lift-and-optimise, recommend a mix, and respond to the CFO.

sub: needs the **least initial change** and **fits the deadline**
but **takes longer** and **costs more up front**
**lift-and-shift for most apps**, **sequenced by dependency and risk**
**optimisation** only for a **few high-cost apps** that can be done in time

items.t: **To the CFO**: year one includes the **migration bubble**

q: Design a portfolio assessment for an organisation with 200 applications and a 2-year programme. How would you decide each app's R, and which app would you migrate first?

sub: the **application concerns**: **performance, architecture, financial, risk, operations, security and compliance**

items: **Diagnose** each app's problem with the **six drivers**
**Assign the lightest R** that fixes it, using the **sourcing and hosting scoring** to decide **who runs it and where**
**Choose the first migration** on the **eight criteria**: **low-risk**, **instructive**, with an **enthusiastic team**, **not the highest ROI**
**Iterate in waves** and compare **TCO against the baseline**

q: An insurer's 30-year-old policy system holds valuable rules, is nearly impossible to change, and is due to be replaced by a SaaS product in 3 years. A new mobile app needs policy data now. Choose between Retain, Encapsulate and Rebuild, and say what changes if the SaaS project is cancelled.

a.lead: **Encapsulate**: expose **policy data and functions through APIs**, hiding the internals.
items: The mobile app can use them **now**; the system **stays in place** until the **planned Replace**
**Not Rebuild** → would **duplicate work** the **SaaS replacement** will make redundant
**Not plain Retain** → would leave the mobile app **without data**
**Risk**: the legacy system's **availability and performance** now **limit the mobile app**

items.t: **If the SaaS project is cancelled**: **revisit the drivers**
sub: a **Rearchitect or Rebuild behind the same APIs** becomes the **long-term path**
the **APIs** let you **swap the implementation** without **breaking the app**

q: A team migrating a 3-tier app proposes containers instead of VMs for the web and app tiers, keeping the database on a VM. Evaluate the proposal, including where containers would be the wrong choice.

items: **Containers**: **lighter**, usually **start faster**, **package the app consistently**, and let **each tier scale on its own**
**Database**: keep it on a **VM** or move it to a **managed database** if it needs **OS-level tuning** or **strong isolation**
**Wrong choice** where a workload needs a **different OS kernel** or **strong tenant separation** → containers **share the host kernel**
a.foot: Actual **startup gains** depend on **image size** and **application initialisation**.

q: A team hands in an architecture made of polished diagrams only. Infrastructure is still set up by hand from a wiki page. Using the instructor's framing, what is missing?

items: **People**: **diagrams** and **views**
**Machines**: **IaC**, **YAML** and **properties files**
**Cloud native**: the **provisioning code is part of the architecture** → without it the design can't be **reproduced** or **checked against what is running**
a.foot: **Add** **versioned IaC and config** alongside the diagrams.

q: A messaging app and a video-streaming service are both being designed by the same team, and a manager wants one standard architecture and stack for both. Is that sensible?

a.lead: **Probably not.** Different **problem types** lead to different **architectures and stacks**.
items: **Messaging**: many **long-lived connections** and **low-latency delivery**
**Streaming**: **large content delivery**, plus **catalogue** and **recommendation** workloads
a.foot: **Share platform tooling** where it helps, but let each **domain's constraints** drive its design decisions.

q: To hit an MVP date, a team skips automated tests and hardcodes config, and records none of it. Six months later, every change breaks something. What went wrong, and what should they have done?

items: **What went wrong**: the shortcuts became **hidden technical debt**, the instructor's **'secret list'**: **future costs** that **stakeholders can't see or prioritise**
Shortcuts can be a **valid trade-off** for an **MVP**
**Should have**: recorded each one in the **backlog** with its **consequence** and a **remediation item**, next to the **functional** and **non-functional requirements**

q: An on-premises three-tier app is moved one-to-one to cloud equivalents (managed DNS, CDN, load balancer, VMs or containers, managed database). What does this gain, and what doesn't it change?

items: **Gains**: **managed components**, possibly with **autoscaling** and **automatic replacement of failed instances**, while keeping the broad **tier structure**
**Doesn't change**: no **independently deployable business services** → **release coordination** and **whole-app scaling** stay the same
a.foot: **Redesign further** only where a specific **delivery or scaling problem** justifies it.

q: The on-premises database pair must survive a server failure. Active-active or active-passive?

sub: A **standby** takes over when the **primary** fails
**Better use of capacity** and **no failover delay**

a.foot: Choose by **write pattern** and **acceptable complexity**.

q: In the cloud-native version, internal calls go through a service mesh using gRPC, and external traffic comes through an API gateway. Why split it this way rather than routing everything through the gateway?

items: **Gateway**: **north-south** concerns at the **edge**: **firewalling**, **throttling**, **identity** and **monitoring** for **public endpoints**
**Mesh**: **east-west** service-to-service traffic with consistent **routing**, **encryption** and **telemetry**
**gRPC**: efficient for **internal calls**
**Internal traffic through the gateway** → adds a **hop** and makes it a **bottleneck** and **single point of failure**

q: A component generates invoices once a night for 10 minutes, and another serves a 24/7 API. Function, container or VM for each?

sub: A **function** if it fits within **execution limits**
Or a **scheduled container job** if it needs **more time** or **runtime control**, since containers can also run **short jobs**

a.foot: Check **startup**, **state** and **cost** rather than assuming the **packaging** decides them.

q: A team runs 60 containers by hand on 8 machines with Docker. Failed containers stay down until someone notices. What does this show about why Kubernetes emerged?

items: **Docker**: made it easy to **build and run single containers**
**Many containers across many machines** → need **scheduling**, **scaling** and **self-healing**
**Kubernetes**: drawing on **Google's Borg and Omega** experience, provides that **orchestration**, with **pluggable runtime, storage and networking**
a.foot: **Cost**: **learning and operating the cluster**.

q: Plan how to evolve a three-tier on-premises web application (DNS, firewall, load-balanced web and app tiers, active-passive database) to a cloud-native architecture in stages. For each stage, say what it gains and what triggers the next one.

sub: **Managed DNS**, **CDN** at the edge, **cloud load balancers**, **VMs or containers** for the tiers and a **managed database**
**Gains**: **managed operations** and possibly **autoscaling**, with little application change
Run **replicas** behind **Kubernetes Services**, with images in a **registry** and **IaC** for everything
Behind an **API gateway**, with a **mesh** for **internal traffic**
Only where **independent delivery or scaling** is a real problem

a.foot: Each stage adds **operational complexity**, so take the next one only when its **trigger** appears.

q: For a new system with a 24/7 order API, a nightly reconciliation job and an image-thumbnail task triggered by uploads, compare VMs, containers and functions, and choose one for each component.

sub: **VMs**: include a **guest OS** and give **OS control**

items: **Order API** → **containers**: **always-on load** and **portability**
**Nightly reconciliation** → a **scheduled container job**, or a **function** if it fits **execution limits**
**Thumbnails** → **functions**: short, **sporadic**, **event-triggered** work **billed per invocation**
a.foot: Choose by **duration**, **startup latency**, **state**, **runtime control** and **cost**, not by **packaging fashion**.

q: You are asked to produce the architecture for a new cloud-native platform. Using the Day 1 framing (what, how, where, and two audiences), outline what the deliverable must contain and how you would keep it from going stale.

items: **What**: a **reference architecture** with **layers**, **components** and how they **interact**
**How**: **decisions** with the **constraints**, **requirements** and **objectives** behind each
**Where**: **data**, **infrastructure**, **application**, **platform**, **security** and **enterprise viewpoints**
**Two audiences**: **diagrams** for **people**; **IaC**, **YAML** and **config** for **machines** → the running system is **generated from the architecture**
**Backlog**: **functional** and **non-functional requirements** and **recorded technical debt**
a.foot: **Keep it from going stale**: the IaC is part of the architecture, so **changes to it go through review** → design and system stay **aligned**.

q: An app moves from one server to 6 load-balanced instances in the cloud, and users start losing their shopping carts between requests. What changed in the persistence problem?

items: **One server**: each instance kept **cart state locally** → worked
**6 load-balanced instances**: requests land on **different instances** → local state fails, carts lost
**Distributed deployment** → you must decide which state is **shared**, **where it lives** and how it **survives an instance failure**
**Fix**: move carts to a **shared store**
a.foot: **Cost**: a **network call per request** + a **new component** that must be available.

q: A team starting a new cloud app with modest load plans four different databases from day one 'because that's cloud-native'. Do you agree?

items: **Cloud deployment** makes **data distribution** an **explicit choice**, not a requirement to use many stores
**Start simple**: a single **managed relational database** may be enough at first
**Add** stores, **partitioning** or **replication** when **access patterns**, **scale** or **availability requirements** justify it
a.foot: **Trade-off**: each addition brings **extra operational complexity**.

q: A legacy hierarchical database makes a new 'all orders for product X across customers' report very slow, because data is reached from customer records down. Why does the relational model help here?

items: **Navigational models** tie access to the **physical tree** → a query that doesn't follow the **parent-child path** has to **traverse everything**
**Relational model** separates how data is **presented** from how it is **stored**
→ the same **normalised tables** can be **joined** in whatever **direction** a new query needs
a.foot: **Cost**: **join work** at query time.

q: A team wants an object database because 'mapping our class hierarchy to tables is painful'. What does history suggest, and what would you propose?

a.lead: **Propose an ORM over a relational database**, or a **document store** if the objects really are **self-contained aggregates**.
items: **History**: **object databases** did address the **object-relational mismatch**, but never won **market share**
**ORM tools** solved much of the mismatch on top of **mature relational databases**
**Example**: flatten an **inheritance hierarchy** into **one table** with a **type column**

q: A finance system needs precise reporting, star schemas and strict integrity, and is expected to grow tenfold in 5 years. Is a relational database still a sound choice?

items: **Mature and precise**: **normalisation**, **ACID**, **SQL** for reporting
**Risk**: its main weakness → **expensive to scale** for very large **distributed workloads**
**Plan for that growth**: **bigger instances**, **read replicas**, **partitioning**, or **NewSQL** later
a.foot: Plan for growth rather than **giving up integrity** now.

q: Using the search example from the lecture, explain why a relational database was a poor fit for a keyword-to-URL lookup at web scale.

items: **Workload**: a huge, **read-mostly lookup** spread across **many servers**
**No need** for **multi-record transactions**, many **entities** or **integrity constraints**
**Relational database** → provides **features the workload doesn't use** + makes the **distribution** it does need **costly**
a.foot: Where **joins and transactions** matter, the **balance reverses**.

q: An IoT platform ingests 50,000 sensor readings a second, and each device type sends a different set of fields. Which of the V's are causing pressure, and what do they point to?

a.lead: **Velocity, Volume, Variety** together point to a **distributed NoSQL store** for the **raw readings**.
items: **Velocity**: **real-time ingestion** needs **distributed persistence** for **throughput**
**Volume**: **scale out** on **commodity or cloud servers**, not one big server
**Variety**: fields differ by device → a **non-static schema** helps
a.foot: Keep any **transactional data**, such as **billing**, wherever its **integrity needs** are best met.

q: A 5-person team proposes a graph database, a document store, a cache and a relational database for an app with 2,000 users. When is polyglot persistence a bad idea, and what would you do?

a.lead: **Bad idea when** the **gain** from a better **storage fit** is smaller than the **cost of programming and operating** each extra technology, likely here given the **team size** and **load**.
items: **Start with fewer stores**
**Add one** only when an **access pattern** clearly needs it
**Wrap data access in services** → a later change has **limited impact**

q: Invoices are always read and written as a whole, with header and line items together, and the format varies by country. Document store or normalised relational tables?

items: **Natural aggregate**: each invoice **maps to one document** → reads need **no joins**
**Varying fields** → no **schema changes** needed
a.foot: **Give up**: easy **cross-invoice constraints** and **ad-hoc joins** (e.g. **reporting across customers and products**) → may need a separate **reporting store**.

q: A social app's 'people you may know' query joins the friendships table to itself three levels deep and is slow. Which pattern fits, and what should you check before switching?

a.lead: **A graph store**: the question is **relationship traversal** across **nodes and edges**, rather than **repeated joins**.
items: **Check** that the real workload is **traversal-heavy**
**Benchmark** it with **realistic data** and **indexes** → graph stores are **not universally faster** than joins
**Keep other data**, such as **profiles**, in whatever store suits it

q: In a column-family store, customer rows have a profile family and an order-history family. A screen reads only the profile. Why does the grouping matter?

items: **Column family**: columns assumed to be **read together** are **stored together** → reading the profile doesn't pull the large **order history**
**Sparse rows**: customers **without orders cost nothing**
**Choose families from the access patterns**
a.foot: A screen that needs **both families in one read** loses this benefit.

q: A game needs a real-time global leaderboard updated thousands of times a second. Which store type fits, and what would you keep elsewhere?

a.lead: **An in-memory key-value store** with **sorted structures** such as **rankings**.
items: **Why**: a leaderboard is **direct keyed access** that must be **very fast**
**Keep elsewhere**: **durable data** such as **player accounts** and **purchases** → a **durable store**
a.foot: A **cache can lose data on failure** unless **persistence is configured**.

q: A team picks a column-family store because 'we'll have terabytes of data'. Is size a good reason, and what should decide it?

a.lead: **No. Data size alone** doesn't decide the **store family**.

sub: **Column-family**: **row-key access** to large **sparse records** grouped into families

items: **Model the access patterns**, then **benchmark the real queries**

q: A payments company needs SQL, strong ACID transactions and horizontal scale across regions. Is NewSQL the obvious answer?

items: **NewSQL** aims to combine **relational and SQL semantics** with **distributed scale**
**Evaluate the coordination cost**: **distributed guarantees** add **latency**, especially **across regions**
**Compare** with a **sharded relational design** and with **NoSQL products** that offer **transactions** at the **scope** you need

q: An analyst asks to run sales reports on the operational column-family store 'because both are columnar, like the warehouse'. What is the misunderstanding?

items: **Column-family store**: groups **sparse, row-keyed records** for **operational access**
**Analytical columnar warehouse**: a **SQL store** built for **large scans** and **aggregations**
**Heavy reports** on the operational store → **perform poorly** + **compete with live traffic**
a.foot: **Feed a warehouse** for analytics instead.

q: An app is overwhelmed by writes. A teammate proposes adding read replicas with master-slave replication. Will it help? What would?

items: **Replicas** add **read capacity**, but **every write** still goes to the **single leader** → **write bottleneck stays**
**Shard** by a suitable key → **independent writes** go to **different servers**
**Peer-to-peer replication** may help some workloads, but each update still has to **propagate** and may need **conflict handling**

q: A regional retailer stores Singapore and Malaysia orders together and has one global product list. How would you distribute each kind of data?

items: **Orders** → **shard by country**: each node handles its **own reads and writes**, spreading both **volume** and **write load**
**Product list** → **replicate to every node**: **read-heavy** and **shared**; **single-leader replication** fits since **writes are rare**
a.foot: **Trade-off**: **cross-country reports** now need to **query several shards**.

q: A bank's product team wants eventual consistency 'everywhere, for scale'. Where would you allow it and where not?

items: **ACID (transactional)**: **authoritative balances** and **transfers** → **temporarily inconsistent** balances are **wrong and costly**
**Eventual consistency (BASE)**: **derived views** such as an **activity feed**, **analytics** or a **product listing** → a **briefly stale read** does little harm
a.foot: State the **consistency requirement per operation** instead of setting **one policy** for the whole system.

q: After switching to peer-to-peer replication, two regions accept conflicting updates to the same customer record during a network split. What caused this, and what are the options?

items: **Cause**: **multiple writers** + **asynchronous propagation** favour **availability** → both regions **accepted writes** and the **copies diverged**

sub: **Home region**: route each record's writes to it
**Coordinated writes** for that data → cost **latency** and **availability during a split**

q: A load-balanced web fleet must share user-uploaded files between instances. Which storage fits, and why not a block volume attached to one VM?

a.lead: **A network file system** if the app needs **shared file semantics**, or **object storage** if it can use **object APIs**.
items: **Object storage** also lets **web and mobile clients** fetch the files
**Not a block volume**: normally a **disk for one attached VM**, not a **shared filesystem**
**Concurrent writers** on it need **explicit support** and **coordination**

q: A team stores its database files on the VM's local instance disk because it is fastest. What is the risk, and what would you change?

items: **Risk**: **instance-store disk** is **ephemeral** → data can disappear on **stop**, **termination** or **host failure**
**Change**: put database files on a **persistent block volume** with suitable **retention** and **backups**, or use a **managed database**
**Local disk**: keep for **scratch data** that can be **regenerated**

q: Images must be served to a web app, a mobile app and a partner's batch job. Why is object storage the natural fit?

items: **Object storage** is reached through a **standard web API** → every **channel** and **service model** uses it the same way, **without mounting a disk**
Also the **most flexible** and **widely used** option
a.foot: **Trade-off**: it isn't a **normal filesystem** → apps that expect **file locking** or **in-place edits** need changes.

q: A team wants to install a database on a VM instead of using the provider's managed relational database 'to keep control'. When is that justified?

a.lead: **Justified when compatibility**, a needed **extension or version**, or a **capability missing** from the managed option justifies the **operating burden**.
items: **Otherwise managed is the better default**: offloads much **maintenance**, **patching**, **backup** and **availability** work
**Either way**, the customer still designs **access**, **schemas**, **capacity** and **recovery**

q: An e-commerce app needs a session cache, a catalogue with varying product attributes, sales analytics and 'customers who bought this also bought' recommendations. Match each to a store type and give the reason.

items: **Session cache** → **in-memory key-value**: **fast keyed access** to **disposable data**
**Catalogue** → **document or key-value**: **attributes vary** per product and items are **read whole**
**Analytics** → **columnar SQL warehouse**: **scans and aggregations**
**Recommendations** → **graph store**: **relationship traversal**
a.foot: Each extra store adds **operational cost** → **drop one** if a **simpler store** meets the need.

q: Design the persistence strategy for a cloud-native e-commerce platform with a catalogue (varying attributes), carts that must survive a cache failure, orders, recommendations and product images. Justify each store and say which one you would drop if the team were only 4 people.

items: **Orders** → **managed relational database**: **ACID transactions**
**Catalogue** → **document store**: **flexible attributes** read as **whole items**
**Carts** → **durable key-value store**, or the relational database, with a **cache in front** → carts must **survive cache loss**
**Recommendations** → **graph store**: **traversal**
**Images** → **object storage** served through a **CDN**

sub: **Drop the graph store** → compute recommendations in **batch** from the **order database**

a.foot: Each extra store adds **programming and operational complexity**.

q: A regional retailer's single relational database can't keep up with growing order writes across Singapore and Malaysia. A teammate proposes read replicas. Evaluate that, then propose how to scale the data tier and name two side effects to monitor.

sub: Won't fix a **write bottleneck** → all writes still go to **one leader**
**Shard orders by country** → each node serves its **own reads and writes**
**Replicate** the **shared, read-heavy product list** to both nodes with **single-leader replication**
Keep **payment data under ACID**; accept **eventual consistency** only where the **business allows**
**Replica lag** on the product list (**stale prices**)

q: Recommend data stores for a global banking ledger and for a social media status feed, and explain why the SQL versus NoSQL label alone doesn't settle the choice.

items: **Ledger** → a **relational or NewSQL store** fits: needs **transactional invariants** and **durability**; weigh **distributed coordination cost** against **scale needs**
**Feed** → a **distributed NoSQL store** with **eventual consistency**: tolerates **briefly stale replicas**, needs high **write and read scale**
a.foot: Decide from **per-operation consistency requirements**, **access patterns** and **coordination cost**.

q: A manager says 'NoSQL replaced relational databases, so all new systems should be NoSQL.' Using the V's of big data and the web-search example, explain why NoSQL emerged and argue whether the claim holds.

items: **Web-search lookup**: needed none of the **joins** or **multi-record transactions** that relational systems provide
**Claim doesn't hold**: relational databases remain the **natural fit** for **constraints**, **joins** and **ACID transactions**
**Polyglot persistence**: use **each model where it fits**
a.foot: Accept the **complexity** only when the **benefit is larger**.

q: An image-processing service has 10 worker VMs. Choose storage for temporary processing scratch space, the job database's data files, configuration shared by all workers, and finished images served to web and mobile apps. Then say what breaks if the shared configuration is put on one VM's block volume.

items: **Scratch** → **ephemeral instance disk**: it can be **regenerated**
**Database files** → **persistent block volume** with **retention** and **backups**, or a **managed database**
**Shared configuration** → **network file system**
**Finished images** → **object storage**, reached through its **API** by both apps

items.t: **Shared config on one VM's block volume**
sub: A block volume is normally **attached to one VM** → the **other 9 workers** couldn't read the configuration
**That VM's failure** would take the configuration with it

q: A company moved its app onto Kubernetes on a public cloud, but releases still happen quarterly by hand and nobody watches metrics. Is it cloud native? Use the three Ps.

items: **Properties** missing: **observable**, **resilient**, **loosely coupled**
**Practices** missing: **automation**, **continuous delivery**, **DevOps**
→ it gets little of the **speed**, **resilience** or **scale** that cloud native aims for
a.foot: Add **CI/CD**, **monitoring** and **automated recovery** before calling it cloud native.

q: A team says 'we use only open-standard containers, so we have no lock-in.' Do you agree?

items: **Open standards** → tools easier to **integrate**, can lower **switching costs**
**Lock-in also comes from provider-specific APIs**, **managed data services** and **operational dependencies**
**Check** each **managed service** the app uses, and how its **data would move**, before claiming **portability**

q: During a zone failure, an app's autoscaler added capacity but users still saw errors for 20 minutes. Which cloud-native property was missing, and why isn't autoscaling enough?

a.lead: **Resilience** was missing: the ability to **continue or recover after failure**.
items: **Autoscaling** adjusts **capacity to demand** only
It doesn't **reroute traffic** around a **failed zone** or replace **dependencies** that went down with it
**Resilience needs design work**: **multi-zone placement**, **health checks**, **failover**, **bounded retries**

q: A new service processes uploaded documents within seconds of arrival, runs a few hundred times a day, and needs no special runtime. Another holds long-lived WebSocket connections. CaaS or FaaS for each?

items: **Document processor → FaaS**: **short, event-driven** work; the platform handles **runtime** and **autoscaling**; you **pay only when it runs**
**WebSocket service → CaaS**: **long-running** and needs **runtime control**, something **functions handle poorly**
a.foot: **Trade-off**: FaaS gives up **control** and **portability**; CaaS keeps them but **you operate more**.

q: A team chose managed Kubernetes and says they no longer have any infrastructure work. Is that right?

items: **CaaS** manages the **container platform components**
**Worker-node operations** such as **patching** and **scaling** may still fall to the **customer**, depending on the offering
**Data accountability** always stays with the customer
**Check** the provider's actual **responsibility split**
a.foot: '**Favour managed services**' moves effort to **business code** but doesn't remove all operations.

q: A container image passed every test in staging but fails in production with the same image tag. What is the most likely cause?

items: The **image fixes** the **app and dependency versions** only
**Behaviour also depends on** external **configuration**, **platform features** and **backing services** → these **differ between staging and production**
**Compare environment config**, **secrets**, **service endpoints** and **platform versions**
a.foot: Keeping **dev and prod sufficiently alike** reduces this.

q: A web tier uses sticky sessions with session data held in instance memory. During a scale-in event, users are logged out. Diagnose it and fix it.

items: **Diagnosis**: **scale-in** removed instances that held the **only copy** of some sessions → **sticky routing** sent users to sessions that **no longer existed**
**Fix**: move **session state** to a **shared store**, or use suitable **client-held tokens** → any **ready instance** can serve the next request
a.foot: **Cost**: a shared store on the **request path** that must itself be **available**.

q: A team runs a database in Kubernetes with a StatefulSet. A reviewer suggests a managed external database instead. When is each right?

items: **External managed database** → usually the **better default**: the provider handles **backups**, **replication** and **patching**; the cluster stays **stateless**
**StatefulSet**, or an **Operator** that encodes **operational knowledge** → right when the store must **run in the cluster** for **control** or **portability**, and the team **accepts operating it**

q: A teammate says 'we're on containers, so our servers are cattle now.' What would show whether that is true?

a.lead: **Pets versus cattle** is an **operating model**, not a technology.
items: **Check**: can any instance be **deleted and recreated from automation** without **losing data** or needing someone to **fix it by hand**?
**Containers** that are **patched in place** or hold **unique local state** → still **pets**
**Disposable VMs** can be **cattle**

q: A team rebuilds the image separately for test and for production with different config baked in. Which factors does this break, and what is the risk?

a.lead: Breaks **build/release/run separation** and **config in the environment**.
