Its **side effects** are hard to reason about (a **charge without an email**)
**Fix**: split into a **push-based pipeline** in which each step **triggers the next through events**
a.foot: **Cost**: **coordinating the steps** and handling a **failure part-way through**.

q: A video platform transcodes uploads that arrive in bursts of hundreds after events, with nothing in between. Is serverless a good fit, and why?

a.lead: **Yes**: **data processing and transcoding** is a **typical use case**.
items: Work is **triggered by events**
Can run **in parallel** on **stateless compute**
**Pay only during bursts**
a.foot: Check the platform's **execution time and memory limits** against the **longest video**; very long transcodes may need a **container or batch service** instead.

q: An order workflow can take hours while waiting for warehouse confirmation. Must one function stay running throughout?

items: **Persist workflow state** in a **durable store**
Use **events or scheduled steps** to invoke **short functions** as each piece of work becomes ready
a.foot: A **long-running service** is justified only if the work truly needs **continuous execution** or the **orchestration overhead** outweighs its benefit.

q: A latency-critical API runs at a steady 3,000 requests a second all day. A teammate argues serverless will be cheaper and faster. Evaluate this.

items: **Cheaper?** **Steady high load** → the **pay-per-invocation advantage shrinks** → compare **sustained-use cost** against **always-on containers**
**Faster?** **Cold starts** and **runtime restrictions** can threaten **tight latency budgets**
a.foot: Serverless still fits the **sporadic parts** around this API, such as **scheduled reports** or **file processing**.

q: When an order is placed, three components must react (email, analytics, loyalty), and one invoice job must be handed to exactly one worker reliably. Which serverless compute services fit each?

items: **Events** → the **order notification**: they **broadcast** information to **one or more** interested components
**Tasks** → the **invoice job**: they **reliably deliver** a message to a **single component**
a.foot: Swapped: **events for the invoice** risk **several workers** processing it; **tasks for the notification** mean sending **one task per consumer**.

q: A team needs a containerised HTTP service with a library that won't run in the function runtime, but it doesn't want to manage servers. What serverless compute option fits?

items: Like functions, but **containerised** and **reachable over HTTP**
Team **controls the runtime in the image**; the platform handles **servers and scaling**
a.foot: **Trade-off**: a **larger deployable** and possibly **slower starts** than a function.

q: A small analytics team wants to run SQL over files in object storage once a week without running any servers. How do serverless data services help, and what should they check?

items: **Blob storage** for the files
A **serverless big-data query engine** runs **SQL** over them
→ **nothing runs between queries**; **billing follows usage**
**Check**: the **cost model** and **file formats**
Compare providers by **category and semantics**, not by **one-to-one product names**

q: A mobile app must use a legacy SOAP service that can't be changed. How would you expose it with serverless components, and what remains a risk?

items: **API gateway** in front → presents a **REST interface**
**A function per route**: converts the request to **SOAP/XML**, calls the legacy service, **converts the response**
The **legacy system stays unchanged**
a.foot: **Risk**: its **capacity and latency** now limit the mobile app, because functions **scale far faster** than it can → add **throttling or caching** at the gateway.

q: Clickstream events arrive at 20,000 a second for real-time dashboards. Sketch a serverless pipeline and name one thing to monitor.

a.lead: Pipeline (it **scales with event volume** without servers):
items: Events go into a **stream service**
**Functions pull batches**, **transform** them and **write** to **storage or a database**
The **dashboards query** that store
a.foot: **Monitor**: **consumer lag** and the **write capacity of the target store**, because **fast-scaling functions** can **overwhelm a database downstream**.

q: An architect insists the whole system must be serverless, including a steady, stateful matching engine. What would you propose instead?

a.lead: **A hybrid**: serverless doesn't have to be **all or nothing**.
items: **Fan out events** through **notification topics** into **queues**
Queues consumed by **functions** for **spiky, event-driven work**
... and by **server-based instances** for the **steady, stateful matching engine**
A **shared database** behind
a.foot: Put each part where it is **cheapest** and **fits best**.

q: A business case claims moving an upload workflow to functions will 'cut costs by 60%' based only on compute prices. What is missing from the assessment?

items: **Downstream capacity**: can the **database** absorb the **scaled-out writes**?
**Retry behaviour** and **duplicate processing**
**Added latency**
**Data durability**
**Integration cost**
a.foot: **Operational savings** can be real, but **compute price alone** can't establish them → **model the full request path** at **expected and peak load**.

q: A function that resizes images runs at 128 MB memory and takes 8 seconds, often timing out. A teammate says raising memory will only raise cost. Do you agree?

items: On **function platforms**, **memory also sets the CPU share** → more memory can make the function **finish much faster**
**Billing** = **invocations** + **duration weighted by memory** → a shorter run at higher memory may **cost about the same or less**
**Test a few memory sizes**; set the **timeout from the measured duration**

q: A function's execution role has full access to every storage bucket and database 'to avoid permission errors'. What is the risk, and what should the role grant?

items: **Risk**: if the function's code or a **dependency is compromised**, the attacker gets **all of that access**
**Grant only** the **resources and actions** the function needs, e.g. **read from one bucket** and **write to one table**
a.foot: The **execution role** and the **timeout** are the main controls on **what a function can touch** and **how long it can run**.

q: A function is triggered by messages from a queue, and a teammate calls it 'asynchronous, so the caller never waits'. Is that the right way to classify it?

a.lead: **Not quite**: classify the invocation by its actual **delivery and retry contract**.
items: **Queue**: the platform often **polls the source** and invokes the function **in batches** → a **different contract**
**Synchronous call**: the **caller waits** for the result
**Asynchronous call**: an **event is accepted** for **later execution**
a.foot: That contract decides **error handling** and **duplicate processing**.

q: A function exposed through an API gateway logs a successful run, but clients still get an error response. Using the request flow, where would you look?

a.lead: Flow: **method request** → **integration request** → **function execution** → **integration response** → **method response**.
items: The function ran → likely fault in the **integration response** or **method response**
The function's **output wasn't mapped** to a **valid HTTP response**, e.g. a **missing status code** or **wrong body format**
**Check** the function's **logs** and **output format**; **test the stage endpoint** directly

q: A startup's image-upload service is idle at night and gets bursts of 5,000 uploads a minute during campaigns. Should it use serverless? Design it and name two limits or side effects to plan for.

sub: An upload to **object storage** **triggers** a **stateless function**
It **resizes the image** and writes results back to **object storage**

items: **Why it fits**: **scales with bursts**, **bills per invocation**, **no idle servers at night**

items.t: **Limits and side effects to plan for**
sub: **Execution time and memory limits** for **large images**
The **burst of concurrent writes** to the **metadata store**

q: An order system is being designed. A teammate argues for 'pure FaaS, one function per operation'; another wants microservices on containers. Compare the options, recommend one, and explain how they could combine.

items: **Microservices** choose **deployment boundaries** (**Order**, **Payment**, **Inventory** as **independently deployed capabilities**)
**FaaS** chooses **how handlers execute**
**One function per operation** → **maximises granularity**, but adds **deployment, monitoring and coordination overhead** and **cold starts** on **latency-sensitive paths**

sub: **A few functions** where load is **spiky and event-driven** (**notifications**, **receipts**)

a.foot: Assess **state**, **latency**, **limits** and **coordination cost**, not **function count**.

q: Design a serverless back end that lets a mobile app use a legacy SOAP order system that handles at most 50 requests a second. Explain how you would protect the legacy system and secure the functions.

items: **API gateway** in front of the mobile app with **REST routes**, each invoking a **function** that translates to **SOAP/XML** and back
**Authentication** at the gateway or through a **managed identity service**

sub: Send **non-urgent writes** through a **queue** that a function **drains at a controlled rate**

items: **Secure the functions**: give each an **execution role** limited to **what it calls**
a.foot: **Trade-off**: **queued writes** are **confirmed later**, not immediately.

q: A team asks when serverless is the wrong choice. Give three workload characteristics that argue against it, and for each say whether a redesign could still make functions work.

sub: **Redesign**: functions still work if the work can be **split into short steps** with **state persisted** between them

items.t: **Tight latency budgets** that **cold starts** would break
sub: A **long-running service** is usually the **simpler answer**

items.t: **Steady high load** where **sustained-use cost** exceeds **always-on compute**
sub: **Compare costs**; the honest answer is often **containers**

items: **Stateful work** that depends on **one instance's memory** → can be redesigned with **external durable state**

q: Design a serverless real-time analytics pipeline for 20,000 click events a second with dashboards updated within 10 seconds, and say what happens when a downstream database slows down.

sub: Events enter a **stream service** **partitioned for throughput**
**Functions consume batches**, **transform and aggregate** them, and write to a **database or storage** that the **dashboards query**
**Raw events** also go to **object storage** for **later reprocessing**
**Function retries** and **consumer lag** grow → the **dashboards fall behind**

a.foot: Accept that the dashboards may **briefly exceed 10 seconds** rather than **overloading the database**.

q: A team training a language model on a large corpus finds an RNN takes weeks because each step waits for the previous one. Why would a Transformer train faster on the same hardware?

items: **RNN**: passes context through **recurrent state** one step at a time → training can't be **parallelised** across a sequence
**Self-attention**: connects positions directly → computation over the **known training input** can run **in parallel**, which suits **GPU** hardware
**Long-range links**: also links **distant words** without passing through every step in between

q: A colleague says 'Transformers process everything in parallel, so a chatbot built on one generates its whole answer at once'. Is that right?

a.lead: **No.** Parallelism applies to **training** over known inputs.
items: **Autoregressive** Transformer (such as a **GPT-style** model) still generates output **token by token**
Each new token **predicted from the context so far**
→ **response time grows** with answer length
→ **streaming** the output token by token is common in chat applications

q: In 'The animal didn't cross the street because it was tired', explain how self-attention gives 'it' the right meaning, and what would change in 'because it was too wide'.

items: **Query** for 'it' is scored against every word's **Key**
**Softmax** turns the scores into **weights**
**Weighted sum of Values** → 'it' gets a representation built mostly from **'animal'**
**'because it was too wide'**: the context changes the scores → **'street'** would get the higher weight
a.foot: The weights are **learned from data**, not fixed rules.

q: What would go wrong if the attention scores were used directly as weights, without softmax?

items: **Raw scores**: on an **arbitrary scale** and can be **negative**
→ the weighted sum of Values would not be a **proper average**; could be dominated by **scale rather than relevance**
**Softmax**: turns the scores into **positive weights that sum to 1** → output is a **weighted average** that favours the best-matching words

q: A text-generation model must not use words that come later in the sentence when predicting the next word, but a translation model's encoder can read the whole source sentence. How does attention differ between them?

items: **Generating decoder**: **causal attention** → **masks future positions**, so each token attends only to earlier ones
**Encoder**: **self-attention** can use the **whole input**
**Encoder-decoder** models: also **cross-attention** → the decoder's **queries** can look at the **encoder's outputs**

q: An HR chatbot built on a plain LLM call gives confident but outdated answers about this year's leave policy. Which pattern fixes this, and why not retrain the model?

items: **RAG**: retrieve the **current policy documents** and add them to the **prompt** → answers **grounded** in the company's own, **up-to-date** data
**Plain LLM**: only knows its **training data** plus the prompt
**Retraining**: **costly** and goes **stale** again with the next policy change; updating the **document index** is cheap
a.foot: Keep the index current, because RAG is **only as fresh as its sources**.

q: A RAG assistant retrieves the refund policy correctly. The business now wants it to issue refunds as well. What changes in the design, and what new risk appears?

items: **Tool selection**: the model selects tools, such as calling the **order and payment service APIs**
**Multi-step**: acts over several steps, still using **retrieval** for policy
**New risk**: retrieval gave the model **information, not permission**
**Safeguards**: each tool needs **authorisation checks**, **limits** such as a **refund cap**, and **logging**, with **human approval** for high-value actions

q: A team building an agent that calls two internal APIs says it must first set up a vector store for memory. Is that required?

items: **Lecture's agent architecture**: an **interface**, a **model**, **instructions** or a **prompt recipe**, **planning**, **tool integrations**, **memory or context**
**Tool-using agent with short tasks**: may need only **conversation context**
**Add a vector store** when the agent must retrieve from a **large document set**

q: A RAG assistant cites a company document but still gives a wrong answer. Give two likely causes and how you would confirm each.

items: **Stale or irrelevant passage** retrieved → confirm: check the **retrieved chunks** and their **dates**
**Model misread correct context** → confirm: check whether the answer is actually **supported by the retrieved text**
a.foot: Retrieval is **not a correctness guarantee**, so evaluate **retrieval quality** and **answer support** separately.

q: A design team wants a model that generates realistic product images, and is comparing a GAN with a diffusion model. Explain how each generates, as the basis for the comparison.

sub: Trains a **generator** against a **discriminator** that tries to tell real images from generated ones
Generates in **one pass** from the trained generator
Generates by **progressively denoising** a random sample over **many steps**

a.foot: The comparison: **adversarial training** vs **iterative denoising**.

q: A hospital must keep patient text inside its own environment, but wants to summarise clinical notes with a language model. Closed model through an API, or open-weight model self-hosted?

a.lead: **Open-weight model, self-hosted** in the hospital's environment.
items: **Fits the data constraint**: the **released weights** allow deployment and **tuning** under their **licence** without sending notes to a provider
**Cost**: operating **GPUs**, **capacity**, **updates** and **reliability**
**Closed API**: ready to use but **ties you to the provider** and sends data **outside**
a.foot: A closed API fits only if its **terms** and **deployment options** meet the constraint.

q: A startup plans to train its own foundation model for customer-support answers. What does the GenAI stack suggest instead?

a.lead: Most teams add value **higher up the stack**.
items: **Foundation models**: **expensive to pre-train** but **reusable** across many tasks
**Customisation**: **prompt engineering**, **RAG** or **fine-tuning**
**End-to-end application**
a.foot: Training their own model is justified only for a **capability** or a **data constraint** that existing models can't meet.

q: A bank wants to cut call-centre wait times with GenAI. Which application fits, and what must be added for it to be accurate?

a.lead: An **AI phone agent**: **speech interaction** + a **language-model service** that handles **routine enquiries**.
items: **Voice generation alone** is not enough
**Accuracy**: answers must come from **maintained knowledge sources** (**RAG**)
**Account actions**: need **authorised tools**
**Handoff to a human** for complex or sensitive cases

q: A marketing team wants lip-synced localised versions of a training video in 12 languages, plus a brand jingle. What does the architect need to check before treating these as simple API calls?

a.lead: Each capability can be consumed as a **service through APIs**, but check:
items: **Quality review for each language**: **translation** and **lip-sync errors** are public
**Usage and licence terms** for generated **voice**, **likeness** and **music**
**Cost and turnaround** at scale
**Human approval step** in the workflow before **publication**

q: Design a GenAI customer-support assistant for a cloud-native e-commerce platform that must answer from current product and policy documents and also check order status. Choose plain LLM, RAG or agent, and say how it fits into the existing microservices.

a.lead: **RAG** for answers, extended to an **agent** for order status.
items: **RAG**: retrieve current **product docs**, **FAQs** and **policies** from an index such as a **vector store** → responses **grounded** without retraining
**Agent tools**: **order status** by calling the **order service's existing API** with the **customer's own authorisation**
**Refunds** stay behind **human approval**
**Fit with microservices**: run the assistant as **its own service** behind the **API gateway**, using a **hosted foundation model** through an API or a **self-hosted open-weight** model
**Monitor** **retrieval quality** and **answer support**
a.foot: Retrieval **doesn't guarantee correctness**.

q: Explain the layers of the GenAI tech stack, and advise a 10-person cloud-native team on where to invest and where to buy.

sub: Where the team's **data** and **domain knowledge** create value

a.foot: Choose **closed versus open weights** by **data constraints** and **operating capacity**.

q: An enterprise wants GenAI for expense processing: answer staff questions about the policy, read receipt images and submit claims. Compare a plain LLM, RAG and an agent for this, and design the safeguards for the part that acts.

items: **Plain LLM**: can interpret text but doesn't know the company's **current policy**
**RAG**: adds the **retrieved policy** → enough for **staff questions**
**Agent** with **tools** calling the **expense system's API**: needed for **extracting receipt data** and **submitting claims**

sub: Tools act only with the **employee's permissions**
**Limits** route claims above a **threshold** to **human approval**
Agent can only **prepare or submit** within **defined integrations**

a.foot: The patterns **combine**, but **an answer is not a permitted business action**.

q: A product manager asks why chat responses get slower as answers get longer, even though 'Transformers are parallel'. Explain using the RNN-to-Transformer change, and give one design implication for a cloud-native chat service.

items: **RNN → Transformer**: step-by-step **recurrence** replaced by **self-attention**
**Training**: runs **in parallel** over known inputs and links **distant context** directly → made **large-scale training** possible
**Generation**: still **autoregressive**; each token predicted from the tokens so far → a **longer answer takes longer** to generate
**Design implication**: **stream tokens** to the client as they are generated; set **timeouts** and **capacity** by **expected output length**

q: A global marketing organisation proposes three GenAI features: personalised video per customer segment, first-draft product copy in 8 languages, and AI-generated ad music. Assess each for business value and risk, and say what process control is needed across all three.

sub: Risk: **costliest** to generate; most **likeness** and **brand risk**
Risk: its **usage terms** must permit **commercial use**

items: **Common business value**: **content at scale**, **personalisation**, **faster delivery**
a.foot: **Process control** across all three: **human review and approval** before **publication**, and **track the usage terms** of each generated asset.

q: A team's security budget goes entirely to preventive controls (firewalls, WAF, hardening), with no log retention or alerting. Using the lecture's figures on time to identify and contain breaches, critique this.

items: **Cited figures**: historical averages of about **206 days to identify** and **314 days** from breach to **containment** (which includes the 206)
→ intrusions often stay active **for months**
**Prevention alone**: leaves no way to **notice** or **investigate** one
**Fix**: move some budget to **retained, protected logs** and **audit trails**, **alerting**, and an **incident response process** → shorten that window

q: An online store suffers two incidents: a flood of requests that makes checkout unavailable for an hour, and an attacker on public Wi-Fi intercepting and altering customers' sessions. Which property does each break, and which control addresses each?

items: **Flood** = **denial of service** → an attack on **availability** → **DDoS protection**, **rate limiting**, **autoscaling headroom**
**Interception** = **man-in-the-middle** → breaks **confidentiality** and **integrity** → enforce **TLS end to end**, with **secure cookies** and **certificate validation**
a.foot: **Naming the property first** points to the right control.

q: The lecture's figures say most breaches are financially motivated. A startup concludes it should spend its whole security budget on encrypting its database. Is that the right inference?

items: **Financial motive** → protect **valuable data** and the **privileged credentials** that reach it
**Encryption at rest** doesn't stop an attacker who steals an **application or admin credential** that can **decrypt**

items.t: **Prioritise** from the system's actual **assets and risks**
sub: Then **encryption** and **tokenisation** where they cut exposure

q: A company moves from IaaS VMs to a SaaS CRM. Which security duties does it stop doing, and which does it keep?

items: **Stops**: **patching and operating** the **OS**, **middleware** and **application**, which the **SaaS provider** now runs
**Keeps**: **data classification**, decisions about **who gets access**, **account management**, **accountability** for its data
**Shared**: **endpoint** and **identity** duties
a.foot: Moving to SaaS shifts **operations, not accountability**.

q: A provider's firewall service worked as designed, but a rule allowing all inbound traffic exposed a database. Who is responsible, and what does this example show?

items: **Provider**: responsible for the **firewall service working**
**Customer**: responsible for **configuring its rules**
→ a **joint control**, where each side owns a different part
a.foot: **Audit and review rules as code** to catch this kind of **misconfiguration**.

q: A provider passes every security audit, but a government agency still hesitates to move. Give two concerns that the provider's security can't resolve, and what would address each.

items: **Regulation and legislation** about where data may live and who can access it → **in-country regions** or a **hybrid placement**, with **contract terms**
**Ownership, control and trust** → **key control**, **exit terms** and **audit rights** in the contract
a.foot: Another concern: lack of **in-house cloud skills** → **training** or a **partner**.

q: A developer commits a cloud access key to a public repository, and it is misused within 36 hours. Using STRIDE, what could happen, and what limits the damage?

sub: **Elevation of privilege** if the role can **grant more access**

items: **Least privilege** → limits **what** the key can do
**Short-lived credentials** and **rotation** → limit **how long**
**Audit trails** → support **investigation**
**Secret scanning** in the **pipeline** → prevents the commit in the first place

q: A public API that returns tax records was abused to pull hundreds of thousands of records, as in the IRS 'Get Transcript' case. Which controls would have reduced the risk?

a.lead: Treat the **API as an attack surface**:
items: **Strong authentication** and **per-record authorisation**
**Input validation** and **application security testing**
**Rate limiting** and **monitoring** for **abnormal access patterns**
A **WAF**
**Incident response** able to **detect bulk extraction** quickly
a.foot: Any **single control alone** would have left gaps.

q: A company chooses a private virtualised cloud 'so we are safe from shared-technology vulnerabilities like VENOM'. Is that reasoning sound?

items: **Multi-tenancy** in **public cloud** amplifies the risk: a **guest escape** to the **hypervisor** can reach **other customers' workloads**
**Private virtualised** environments share the **same class of risk** across their own workloads
Still matter: **patching hypervisors** and **separating high-sensitivity workloads**

q: A small storage provider your firm depends on announces it is closing and gives customers two weeks to move their data. What should you have done beforehand?

a.lead: This is the **insufficient due diligence** threat.
items: **Due diligence** on the provider's **financial and operational stability**
**Exit and data-return terms** in the **contract and SLA**
**Backups** held **independently** of the provider
A **tested portability plan** that avoids **deep lock-in**
a.foot: The **Nirvanix** case shows how **short the notice** can be.

q: One incident: an outsider steals an admin's password through a phishing page and logs in. Another: a database administrator copies customer records before resigning. Classify each and give the most relevant control.

items: **Phishing then login** = **account hijacking**: an **outsider** takes over a **legitimate account** → **strong multi-factor authentication** and **anomaly detection**
**DBA copying records** = **malicious insider**, who already has **legitimate access** → **least privilege**, **no shared admin accounts**, **activity monitoring**, **prompt deprovisioning**
a.foot: Both are **breaches** (**disclosure**), not **data loss**.

q: Customer support staff need to verify the last 4 digits of a card, and a payments service needs to process refunds. Masking or tokenisation for each?

items: **Support → masking**: the screen shows only the **last 4 digits**, hiding the rest from viewers
**Payments → tokenisation**: systems store and pass a **token**; only the **protected vault** that holds the **mapping** can recover the **real number**
a.foot: Both **reduce exposure** but still need **access controls**, and their **compliance effect** depends on the design.

q: A team says its data is safe 'because we use BYOK'. What should you check?

a.lead: Check **who can actually use the key to decrypt**.
items: **BYOK**: the **customer supplies the key**, but the **provider's service** may still use it to **process data** → doesn't prove the provider **can't decrypt**
Check **key-use permissions**, **recovery** and **revocation**
Check whether **customer-held keys** are needed
a.foot: **Customer-held keys** mean the provider may be **unable to process** the encrypted data.

q: Encrypted-at-rest customer data leaks through an application endpoint that returned other users' records. Why didn't encryption help, and what would have?

items: **Why encryption didn't help**: the running **application is authorised to decrypt** and read the data → **encryption at rest** protects **stored media**, not **misuse by an authorised process**
**Needed**: **authorisation checks on each record**, **least-privilege data and key permissions**, **access monitoring**
a.foot: Encryption **complements** access control; it doesn't **replace** it.

q: A company relies on crypto-shredding to destroy a closed customer's data. What could make it fail?

a.lead: **Crypto-shredding** works only if **no usable decryption keys or plaintext copies** remain.
items: **Plaintext** in **backups**, **logs**, **caches** or **analytics exports** → data still readable
A key that was **replicated elsewhere** → data still readable
**Fix**: apply the **retention policy** and **key destruction** across **every copy**
a.foot: This is why **classification at creation** matters.

q: An employee tries to download the full customer database at 3 a.m. from a personal laptop in another country. Which access-control attributes should influence the decision, and what is a sensible outcome?

items: **Actor**: is this employee allowed this data?
**Function**: **bulk download**, not just viewing
**Location**: a **personal** rather than **company machine**, and a **country** that may break **data-export rules**
**Time of day**
a.foot: **Outcome**: **deny** the request, or require **step-up verification** and limit it to **viewing**; enforce through **IAM** and **federated identity**, not ad-hoc checks.

q: A team protects its app with security groups only and asks why it would also need a WAF. What do you tell them?

items: **Security groups**: filter **network connections** by **address and port** → allow any request on an allowed port, including **malicious HTTP payloads** such as **SQL injection**
**WAF**: inspects **HTTP content**
a.foot: **Layer** them with **host firewalls** and **provider DDoS protection**, because each covers a **different boundary**.

q: Security reviews happen only before release, and last quarter a vulnerable base image reached production. What would you change?

items: **Scan** **application code** and **container images** in the **pipeline** on **every build**
**Fail builds** on serious findings → security **built into delivery** rather than checked at the end
**Mission-critical apps** get **stricter gates**
a.foot: **Cost**: **slower pipelines** and time spent **triaging false positives**.

q: A payments team must protect signing keys so that even a compromised admin can't copy them. Would an HSM meet the requirement, and what does it not guarantee?

items: **HSM**: keeps keys and **cryptographic operations** inside a **tamper-resistant hardware boundary** → keys can be **used but not extracted**
**Not guaranteed**: it doesn't stop a **compromised identity** from **asking the HSM to sign**
a.foot: **Access policy**, **key handling** and **monitoring of HSM use** still matter.

q: A production database was deleted overnight. Would you look in monitoring metrics or in audit events to find who did it, and what can't the record tell you?

items: **Audit events**: record **identity and resource actions**, such as a **delete call** and the **role or user** that made it
**Monitoring metrics and logs**: show the **symptoms** and **timing**
**Limit**: the record identifies the **identity, not necessarily the person**, because the **credential may have been compromised**
a.foot: Audit logs must be **retained** and **protected from tampering**.

q: A contractor left 6 months ago, and their account was used last week to read sensitive files. Which IAM function failed, and what process would prevent it?

a.lead: **Deprovisioning**: access wasn't removed when the person left.
items: Tie **account removal** to the **HR offboarding** process
**Review access** regularly
Prefer **federated identity** or **single sign-on** → disabling one identity removes access **everywhere**
a.foot: **Leftover accounts** are an easy path for **insiders** and **hijackers**.

q: A CIO says: 'We moved to the cloud, so the provider handles security now.' Using the deck's conclusions, correct this.

items: **Provider**: secures the **infrastructure** and supplies **network**, **device**, **identity** and **encryption services**
**Shared responsibility**: the **customer always owns its data** and **how it is accessed**
**Focus shifts to data security**: **classify** data, protect it **in transit, at rest and in use**, and control access throughout its **lifecycle**
The **SLA** defines what the provider **actually commits to**

q: A healthcare provider plans to move its patient records system to a public cloud PaaS. Patient data must stay in the country, and the regulator wants proof of who accessed which record. Propose the security architecture and say which duties remain the provider's.

items: **Placement**: **classify patient data**, use an **in-country region**, confirm the **PaaS responsibility split**
**Encryption**: **TLS** in transit and encrypt **at rest**; decide **who holds and can use the keys**, since **BYOK** and **customer-held keys** differ
**Access**: **least-privilege identities** for **users and services**; **mask or tokenise identifiers** in **non-clinical views**
**Edge**: a **WAF** and **provider DDoS protection** in front
**For the regulator**: retain **protected audit events** and **database activity monitoring per record**

sub: **Classification**, **access decisions** and **accountability** stay with the **healthcare provider**

q: A misconfigured storage bucket leaked customer data. The provider's service worked as documented. Using the shared responsibility model, explain who is accountable, then give a cause, a countermeasure and its drawback.

items: **Provider** secures the **storage service** itself; the **customer** secures **what is in it**, including **configuration**, **access control** and **data classification**, just as with the **firewall example**
**Cause**: a **public-access setting** applied **by hand**
**Countermeasure**: define **bucket policies** in **reviewed IaC**, **block public access by default**, and **alert on policy changes**
**Drawback**: **slower changes** and **friction** for teams that legitimately **publish public content**

q: A microservices application exposes 30 public APIs, and its developers keep cloud keys in config files. Pick three Treacherous Twelve threats most relevant here, explain each through STRIDE, and give mitigations.

sub: **Authenticate and authorise every call**, **validate input**, **rate-limit**, add a **WAF**

items.t: **Insufficient identity, credential and access management** (**spoofing**, **elevation of privilege**)
sub: Move keys to a **secrets manager** and **rotate** them
Use **least-privilege roles** and **scan repositories** for secrets

a.foot: Throughout: run **DevSecOps scanning** of **code and images**, and keep **audit trails** to address **repudiation**.

q: Design data protection across the full lifecycle for a fintech's customer documents (ID scans, statements), including how deletion requests are honoured.

items: **Create**: **classify** ID scans as **sensitive**
**Store**: **encrypt** with **controlled key use**, **restrict access**, **back up** and **monitor**
**Use**: **DLP**, **database activity monitoring**, and **masking** in **support tools**
**Share**: **TLS**, **VPN** or **SSH** channels, and **DLP** or **rights controls** for **external parties**
**Archive**: a **retention policy** with **encryption** and **retrievability**

sub: Only works if **backups**, **logs** and **analytics copies** hold **no plaintext** and the **keys are truly destroyed**

a.foot: **Access follows classification** at every stage.

q: A bank's board asks whether to use public, private or hybrid cloud 'for security'. Argue that the deployment model alone doesn't decide this, and recommend an approach.

a.lead: The **deployment model alone** doesn't decide security.
items: **Security depends on** **data location**, **access control**, **key management**, **provider duties** and **recovery**, not on the **label**
**Public cloud** can meet **sensitive requirements**; **private cloud** still needs all of these controls
**Hybrid** if specific data must **legally stay on premises**: **controlled, encrypted connectivity** and **tokenisation** so public-cloud services handle **tokens rather than raw data**
**Otherwise**: **public cloud** with **in-region placement** and **customer-controlled keys**
a.foot: Either way, the **bank keeps responsibility** for **data classification** and **access**.

q: Your organisation detected a breach only after 200 days, through a customer complaint. Diagnose the gaps and propose the monitoring, visibility and access capabilities you would add, with the main cost.

items: **Gaps**: no meaningful **alerting**, little **audit coverage**, and probably **stale or over-broad access**
**Monitoring**: **continuous monitoring** with alerts on **unusual data movement** and **database access**
**Visibility**: **audit events** for **identity and resource actions** with **protected, long retention**, and an **incident response process**
**Access**: **review privileges** and **deprovision stale accounts**
a.foot: **Main cost** is **ongoing**: **storing logs** and **triaging alerts** needs **staff**, and **noisy alerts get ignored**, so tune them to the **valuable data first**.

q: In a design review, a teammate proposes a home-grown mechanism for letting clients upload files directly to storage with temporary access. You recognise it as a known pattern. Why does naming it matter?

items: **Naming it** gives the team a **shared vocabulary**
Brings the pattern's known **problem**, **mechanism** and **trade-offs**, such as limiting the **scope and lifetime of the key**
→ the design is easier to **justify** and **review**
a.foot: A **home-grown** version risks rediscovering those trade-offs **in production**.

q: A team's problem is cascading failures between services. Which group of a cloud pattern catalogue would you search first, and what would you expect to find?

items: **Expect**: **Circuit Breaker**, **Retry**, **Bulkhead**, **Health Endpoint Monitoring** → address **failing dependencies**
**Catalogues group the same patterns differently** → pick the one whose grouping matches the **problem category**
**Compare the candidates' trade-offs** instead of applying the first match

q: Twelve services in four languages must all ship logs in one format and route database connections per environment. Would you build this into each app, or use container patterns?

items: **Adapter sidecar**: converts each app's **log output** to the **standard format**
**Ambassador sidecar**: **proxies outbound database connections** to the right target **for each environment**
Both work in **any language** without changing **app code**
a.foot: Cost: **extra containers per pod** and a defined **start and stop order** (a **container chain**).

q: A team patches running containers in place to fix a bug, and the next autoscaling event brings back the bug. Which container properties were ignored?

items: New instances start from the **unchanged image** → **in-place fixes are lost** and instances **drift apart**
**Fix**: build a **new image** with the fix and **roll it out**
→ any instance can be **killed and replaced** by an identical one

q: An order service must notify billing, shipping and analytics, and each team keeps asking the order team to add a new call. Which microservice pattern family helps?

items: The order service **publishes events** to a **broker**; each **consumer reacts on its own**
**New consumers subscribe** without changing the order service
An **event store** can also feed **databases** and **analytics**
a.foot: Cost: **eventual consistency**, and the need for **central logging and tracing** to follow a flow.

q: A service saves an order to its database and then publishes 'OrderCreated' to a broker. Sometimes the save succeeds but the publish fails. How does the lecture's event-sourcing design avoid this, and what doesn't it solve?

items: **The event append is the state change**: **OrderCreated** is written **atomically** to the **event store**
**Subscribers** read that **committed history** → no separate **save-then-publish** step to fall out of sync
**Doesn't solve**: an **external broker** or a **remote subscriber** isn't part of the same commit → integrating with them still needs **reliable delivery**

q: A team wants event sourcing for a simple product-catalogue service 'for the audit trail'. What would you weigh?

items: **Benefits**: **full history** for **audit**; **replay** for **recovery** and **analytics**

sub: **Querying current state** is hard, often needing **CQRS read models**
**Storage grows** because all history is kept

a.foot: For a **simple catalogue**, an **audit log table** may give enough history at a fraction of the complexity.

q: When a recommendation service slows down, the product service's threads all wait on it, and the product pages fail too. Give the cause, a countermeasure and its drawback.

items: **Cause**: **synchronous calls** to a **slow callee** hold **threads** until **resources are exhausted** → the failure **cascades**
**Countermeasure**: a **circuit breaker** counts failures and, past an **error-rate threshold**, **trips** → calls **fail immediately**
**Fallback**: such as showing the page **without recommendations**
**Drawback**: while the breaker is **open**, even requests that **might have succeeded are rejected** → **thresholds** and **recovery probes** need tuning

q: Order and Customer services each own their database, and a support screen needs 'all orders with customer names'. Joining across the databases is not allowed. What are the options?

items: **API composition**: a **composer** calls both services and **joins the results in memory** → simple but **slow for large results**
**CQRS**: build a **read-optimised view** from both services' **events** → fast but **lags behind writes**
**Sharing tables**: would make the join easy but **couples the services' releases**

q: An order flow has 7 steps with branching for credit checks, stock and fraud review. Choreography or orchestration for the saga?

items: **Many steps and branches** → a **central orchestrator** keeps the flow in one place where it can be **followed**, **monitored** and **changed**
**Choreography** suits **simple flows** with **few participants**: each service **reacting to events** avoids a coordinator but **scatters the logic**
a.foot: The orchestrator must itself be **durable** and must **not take over the services' business logic**.

q: A saga charges a card, then stock reservation fails, so the saga issues a refund. A teammate calls this 'a rollback'. Why is that misleading?

items: **The charge was committed**: may already have been seen by the **customer** or the **bank**
**A refund is a new business action** with its own outcome and **possible failure**, not an **erasure of history**
**Intermediate states are visible**: a saga isn't one isolated **ACID transaction**
**Design**: **persist saga progress**; make each step and **compensation** **safe to retry**

q: A team uses CQRS without event sourcing, updating the read view from the write database's changes. Is that valid?

items: **CQRS** only separates the **command** and **query models**; it doesn't require **event sourcing** or **separate physical databases** in every implementation
**Event sourcing pairs well** with CQRS: the event store is **poor at queries** and **supplies events to project**
**Without it**: the team must still handle **view lag** and **rebuilding the view**

q: An orders table is sharded by order month, and every December the current shard is overloaded while the others sit idle. Diagnose this and propose a change.

items: **Diagnosis**: **range sharding** on a **sequential key** puts all current writes on the **newest shard** → a **hotspot**
**Change**: **hash sharding** by **order or customer ID** → spreads writes across shards
**Cost**: queries by **date range** now **fan out** to every shard
**Mitigation**: keep a separate **date-indexed read view** if **month reports** are frequent

q: A multi-tenant SaaS has a few very large tenants and must keep EU tenants' data in the EU. Which sharding strategy fits, and why?

a.lead: **Lookup sharding** with **tenant ID** as the **shard key**.
items: The **map** can place each tenant on a **specific shard**
**Residency**: in the right **region**
**Large tenant** → move onto a **dedicated shard**
a.foot: Cost: the **lookup map** becomes a **critical component**, and **tenant moves** need careful **migration**.

q: After hash sharding, one shard is still overloaded. Records are evenly spread. What is the likely cause?

items: One very busy **tenant or item** sends most of the **traffic** to its shard
**Hashing spreads distinct keys**, not the traffic on a single key
**Fix**: **balance by actual traffic**, for example by moving that tenant to **its own shard** with a **lookup**, or adding **caching** for it

q: A bank-grade client of a SaaS product demands strict isolation and will pay extra. Which schema option, and why not the cheaper ones?

items: **Strongest isolation**, **security** and room for **customisation**
**Higher cost** and **fewer tenants per server** → covered by the **premium**
**Separated schema**: shares a **database engine**
**Shared schema**: **co-mingles rows** by **TenantID**
a.foot: The cheaper options may **not meet the client's isolation demand**.

q: A SaaS for small shops has 20,000 tenants, mostly on the same plan, and a few need extra fields. Which schema option fits, and what problem should you expect?

items: **Maximises tenants per server**
**Predefined custom fields** fit if the extra fields are **predictable**
**Problem**: reserved **generic custom columns** that most tenants leave empty → **sparse tables**
**Co-mingled data** → every query must **filter by tenant** → strict **access control** and **testing**

q: A SaaS provider wants enterprise tenants on isolated infrastructure and small tenants sharing everything, all from one codebase. Is that a contradiction?

a.lead: **No.** Multi-tenancy is a **continuum** applied **at each layer**.
items: **Layers**: **deployment** (**bare-metal or VM** versus **shared containers**), **runtime**, **application**, **storage**
**One codebase** with **tenant-specific configuration** can serve **shared** and **isolated tiers**
**Toward isolation**: more **security**, **control** and **customisation** at **higher cost**
**Toward sharing**: **economies of scale**

q: A mobile app on slow networks needs a dashboard built from 5 services. Client or gateway aggregation?

items: **One request instead of five** → suits **limited bandwidth** and **weak devices**
**Hides the internal services**
**Risk**: the combined response **waits for the slowest required service** → set **timeouts** and return **partial results** where the screen allows
a.foot: **Client aggregation** would let parts **render as they arrive**, but costs **five round trips** on a slow network.

q: While a dashboard is aggregated, a discount must be calculated from loyalty tier and basket contents. Should that logic live in the gateway?

a.lead: **No.** It belongs in a **composite microservice** in the **business tier**.
items: **Real-time business logic** during aggregation goes there, not in the gateway
The **gateway** stays focused on **routing** and **cross-cutting concerns**
**Cost**: an **extra hop**, more **code**, more **failure points**; **parallel calls** need **reactive or callback** code

q: A customer-360 view needs orders, support tickets and churn scores from analytics, and must load in under a second. Which aggregation pattern fits, and what does it cost?

items: **Pre-aggregate** into an **operational data store**, often a **document database**
→ the view loads with **one read** and can include **analytics**
**Cost**: **duplicated data**, **extra storage**, **ETL** or **change-data-capture** pipelines
**Freshness**: only as fresh as the **last sync**

q: A payment call from a composite service times out. A developer retries by creating a new payment. What could go wrong, and what is the safe approach?

items: **Risk**: the **timeout doesn't prove the payment failed**; the provider may have **charged** before the response was lost → a new payment can **charge twice**
**Safe approach**: reuse a **stable operation identifier**; **query or reconcile** the original result before **retrying or compensating**
**Coordination layer**: keeps that state in a **persistent store** safe from failure

q: Two services in different teams must both commit or both abort a transfer. One proposes 2PC, the other a saga. What decides it?

a.lead: **The invariant and the participants** decide it.
items: **2PC**: **atomic distributed commit**, but **holds locks**, can **block** when a participant fails, and every participant must **support the protocol**
**Saga**: **local commits** with **business compensations** → reduces **synchronous coupling**, but **exposes intermediate states**
a.foot: If **brief intermediate states** are acceptable to the business, a **saga** usually fits **independent services** better.

q: A composite flow calls 4 services, and one never responds. The flow hangs forever. Which coordination capabilities are missing?

items: **Timeout handling**: a **timer for each flow** that **raises an event** when it expires
**Post-call coordination**: collecting each call's **success or failure** and deciding the **next step**
**State management**: progress **survives a crash**
**Configurable** timers and compensations: different steps need **different limits**

q: Design order processing on microservices where placing an order must reserve customer credit in a separate Customer service. A teammate proposes a shared database to keep it simple. Evaluate that, then design the consistency mechanism and say what users may see.

sub: But **couples** the two services' **schemas and releases** → keep **data private**

items: **Choreograph** it through **events** for this **two-step flow**, or **orchestrate** if steps will grow
**Reliability**: **persist progress**, use **stable command identifiers** and **timeouts**; **compensate** (**cancel the order**) if credit fails
a.foot: **What users may see**: a brief **'pending'** order, because a saga **exposes intermediate states**.

q: A SaaS provider serves 5,000 small businesses and 4 regulated enterprise clients, two of which require in-country data. Propose a multi-tenancy, schema and sharding strategy, and state the trade-offs.

items: **Small tenants**: **shared schema** (**TenantID** with **predefined custom fields**) → **economies of scale**
**Regulated tenants**: **separated database**, or **VM-level isolation**, charged as a **premium tier**
**Lookup sharding** by **tenant ID**: places each tenant, including the **in-country** ones in **local regions**, and can move a **large tenant** to its own shard

sub: Shared side: possibly **sparse shared tables** and **strict tenant filtering**
Isolated side: **higher infrastructure and operating cost**

q: An order-history page must show data from Order, Kitchen, Delivery and Accounting services within 300 ms. API composition is too slow. Design the read side, and decide whether event sourcing is needed.

a.lead: A **CQRS read model**; **event sourcing is optional**.
items: **Order History view** updated from the **four services' domain events** → the page reads **one pre-joined store**
**View lag**: a **just-placed order** may briefly be missing
Handle **duplicate** and **out-of-order events** and **rebuilding the view**
**Event sourcing**: adopt only if **authoritative event history** for **audit and recovery** justifies the **modelling and infrastructure cost**
Otherwise **publish events** from each service's **normal writes**

q: A slow downstream service took down an entire platform last month: gateway threads were exhausted and every API failed. Explain the failure, then design protection at the gateway and between services, naming one drawback.

items: **Failure**: **synchronous calls** to a **slow callee** held **threads** until the **gateway ran out** → one dependency's slowness became **everyone's outage**
**Timeouts** on every call
**Circuit breaker** at the **gateway** and in **callers**: trips past an **error-rate threshold** → calls **fail fast**, with **fallbacks** or **partial responses**
Apply it consistently through **sidecars** or a **service mesh** rather than per-app code
a.foot: **Drawback**: an **open breaker** rejects some requests that would have succeeded, and **badly tuned thresholds** can trip too often.

q: A customer portal home page combines profile, orders, recommendations, support tickets and a churn score. Users are on mobile and desktop. Compare the four aggregation patterns for this page and recommend a combination.

a.lead: **Recommend gateway aggregation** for mobile, with **timeouts** and **partial results**, and **pre-aggregate** the **churn score** and **ticket summary** in the data store.

sub: **Renders parts as they arrive** on desktop
Costs **round trips** on mobile and **exposes coordination in the UI**
Can apply **business logic**, such as **ranking recommendations**

q: A global app's data store has hit single-server limits on write throughput, and EU users' data must stay in the EU. Recommend a sharding approach and name two operational side effects to plan for.

items: **First confirm the limit**: **write compute**, **storage**, **bandwidth** or **geography**
**Lookup sharding** by **region or tenant** → **EU residency**
**Within a region**: **hash by customer ID** → spreads writes and avoids the **hotspots** that **range sharding on dates** would create

sub: **Cross-shard queries and reports** get slower and more complex
**Rebalancing** when shards fill or a **hot key** appears needs **data migration**

a.foot: **Balance by actual traffic**, not record counts.

q: A CIO launches a 'move everything to cloud' modernisation programme because competitors are doing it. Eighteen months later, costs are up and the business sees no benefit. What did Gartner's note warn about?

items: **Warning**: choosing an approach from **fashion** without first **diagnosing** why each application **obstructs the business**
→ the chosen approach **misses the root cause** → **overruns**, **late delivery**, **little benefit** or a **cancelled programme**
**Fix**: a **cause-effect analysis per application** using the **six drivers** before picking an approach

q: A bank's COBOL system must be modernised, but the mainframe contract runs for 8 more years. A teammate says modernisation is impossible until they can move to cloud. Do you agree?

items: **Rearchitect** the **COBOL** code to **Java** and stay on the **mainframe**
Or **replace** the app with an **on-premises COTS package**
a.foot: Pick the approach from the **drivers**, and treat the **hosting location** as a **separate decision**.

q: A board member cites a survey showing CIOs plan more spending on modernisation and cloud and less on legacy infrastructure, and asks to fund all applications equally. What is the flaw?

items: **The trend explains why** portfolios need attention: apps **lose fit and agility** while growing **costlier and riskier**
**But** it doesn't say **which apps need what**
**No one-size-fits-all** fix → **fund by application** after **diagnosis**
Some will need **rebuilding**, some only **replatforming**, and some should be **retained** or **retired**

q: An app's code and features are fine, but it runs on middleware that is going out of support. Which approach fits, and why not rebuild?

items: The problem is in the **technology layer** → replatforming changes it with **minimal code edits**
**Rebuilding** would also change **architecture** and **functionality** that don't need fixing → adds **cost**, **time** and **risk** for **no extra benefit**

q: A legacy claims engine is valuable and stable, but changing it is very risky, and a new mobile app needs its data. Modernise or one of the alternatives?

items: Expose its **data and functions** as **services** through an **API** → the mobile app can use them
The implementation stays **hidden and untouched**
**Extends the app's value cheaply**
a.foot: The **engine's limits remain**, so revisit it later if **business fit** or **agility** becomes the driver.

q: A team proposes rearchitecting an app into microservices because 'users say it is missing features'. Will rearchitecting fix that?

items: **Rearchitecting** changes **technology and architecture** while **preserving behaviour** → limited value for **functional problems**
**Missing features** point to **functionality** → **rebuild** or **replace** can change it
Rearchitect only if the real complaint is the **speed or risk of adding features**, which is an **agility** problem

q: A system can't support a new digital sales channel. What must you diagnose before choosing an approach?

a.lead: Diagnose: missing **business functionality**, or missing **access to existing functions**?
items: **Functionality missing** → **rebuild** or **replace** the component that needs it
**Functions exist but can't be reached** by the new channel → **encapsulating** them behind **APIs** or **integrating at the architecture level** may be enough
a.foot: **Rehosting alone** won't add the capability.

q: Releases of a core app take months and often break unrelated features. Rearchitect or rebuild?

items: **Slow, risky change** points to **agility** and **complexity** → usually from the **architecture**
**Rearchitecting** fixes **architecture and technology** at lower **cost**, **risk** and **disruption** than a **rebuild**
a.foot: **Rebuild** is justified only if the **functionality must also change** or the code **can't be restructured**.

q: Running costs of an app are too high for its value, but users are happy with it. Which drivers and layer does this point to, and which approaches would you shortlist?

items: **Driver**: **IT cost**
**Layer**: most likely **technology**, such as **expensive licences** or **over-provisioned infrastructure**
**Shortlist**: **rehost** or **replatform** → low on **cost**, **risk** and **disruption**
**Not** rebuild or replace: would add **disruption** and **risk** to fix **functionality that already works**
a.foot: **Check the evidence**: drivers **suggest a cause** but don't diagnose it **one-to-one**.

q: A sponsor prefers replacing an in-house HR system with SaaS because it has 'the highest value'. What does the framework add to that view?

items: **Replace**: can change **all layers** and offers **high value**, but causes the **greatest business disruption** → **processes redesigned**, **users retrained**
**Rehost**: low on **value**, **cost**, **risk** and **disruption**, but **changes little**
a.foot: Choose replace only if **business fit** or **innovation** is the driver **and** the business **accepts the disruption**.

q: A large app needs a new customer workflow, but its stable reporting module only needs a supported runtime. Must the whole app be rebuilt?

items: **Workflow component** → **rebuild** or **replace**, where functionality must change
**Reporting module** → **replatform**, where only the **runtime** is the problem
**Confirm dependencies** and **sequence the work** → each change delivers its benefit and **risk stays contained**

q: A sponsor expects replatforming the ERP to make it fit the business better. How do you respond?

items: **Replatforming** changes only the **technology layer** → won't improve **business fit**, which is a **functionality** problem
Gartner: **potential value is often overestimated** in this way
**Set expectations**: if business fit is the driver, **rebuild** or **replace** is needed, with their **higher cost, risk and disruption**

q: Two approaches both fix an app's diagnosed problem: replatform (3 months) and rebuild (14 months, more flexibility). The business wants value this year. Which, and why?

items: Fixes the **actual problem** with **shorter time to value**
**Lower cost of change** and less **execution risk**
Choose a **proportionate change**, not the most extensive one
a.foot: **Rebuild's extra flexibility** is worth it only if a **near-term need for functional change** is expected.

q: A government agency's 20-year-old COBOL benefits system costs too much to run, is hard to change, and its COBOL staff retire within 3 years. The benefit rules themselves still meet policy. Recommend a modernisation approach using the drivers and root-cause layers.

a.lead: **Rearchitect**, for example to **Java**, possibly staying on the current platform.
items: **Drivers**: **cost**, **complexity**, **agility** and **risk** (a **skills shortage** on an **old platform**)
**Root-cause layers**: **technology** and **architecture**, not **functionality**, since the **rules still fit**
**Rearchitecting** **preserves behaviour** while addressing these problems
**Rebuild** only if **restructuring isn't viable**
**Execution**: modernise **component by component**; **encapsulate stable parts** behind **APIs** where **new channels** need them
**Before committing**: compare **time to value**, **cost**, **risk** and **disruption**
a.foot: The **skills deadline** sets the **order of the work**.

q: An on-premises web application has three complaints: hardware is ageing, the database needs constant hand-tuning, and features take months to ship. Compare rehost, replatform and rearchitect for moving it to cloud, and say which complaint each one fixes.

items.t: **Rehost** (**lift and shift** onto **cloud VMs**) → fixes **ageing hardware**
sub: Quickly, cheaply and with the **least risk**

items.t: **Replatform** (e.g. a **managed database** or **managed runtime**, **minimal code changes**) → also fixes **database operations**
**Rearchitect** (e.g. **refactoring into services**) → the only one that fixes **slow feature delivery**

a.foot: **Sensible plan**: **replatform now** and **rearchitect** the **slowest-changing components later**.

q: A company wants to replace its 12-year-old custom CRM with a SaaS product. The sales team is attached to custom workflows. Using Gartner's framework, what should it consider before deciding?

items: **Check the drivers** are **business fit** or **innovation**: replace is justified for **functional gaps**, not for **technology problems** that **replatforming** could fix more cheaply
**Replace**: **high value** but the **greatest business disruption** → **sales processes redesigned**, **users retrained**, **custom workflows may be lost**
**Weigh** **time to value**, **cost** and **execution risk** with **stakeholders**
**Plan** **data migration** and the **retirement** of the old CRM

q: Describe a structured method for selecting modernisation approaches across a 150-application portfolio, and show how it would avoid the failures Gartner describes.

items: **Portfolio assessment**: decide whether each app is **retained**, **retired**, **encapsulated** or **modernised**
**For candidates**: define the issues with the **six drivers**; trace each to its likely **root-cause layer** (**technology**, **architecture** or **functionality**), **checking the evidence**
**Shortlist** approaches that can **change that layer**
**Weigh** **value**, **time to value**, **disruption**, **cost** and **risk** with **stakeholders**
**Execute incrementally** per **component**
a.foot: Avoids **fashion-driven choices** that **miss the root cause** (→ **overruns** and **little benefit**), and avoids **big-bang rewrites**.

q: A migration plan says 'use PaaS', but the architecture diagram shows your team patching VM operating systems, and the IaC creates VMs. What must you clarify before writing more IaC, and why does it matter?

a.lead: Clarify the **service model and responsibility split per component**; a solution can **mix IaaS and PaaS**.
items: **Agree who manages** the **OS, runtime, application and data**
**Make the diagram, migration plan and IaC match** those decisions
**Why it matters**: the responsibility split decides **patching, security and operating cost**
**IaC that contradicts the plan** → turns the mismatch into **running infrastructure**

q: A retailer has 120 on-premises applications and an 18-month data-centre exit. The CIO wants to start with the ERP 'because it gives the biggest saving' and to make everything cloud-native. Critique this plan and propose a first wave.

sub: Starting with a **critical, complex workload** like **ERP**
The **biggest projected saving** is not the right test for a **first project**

items.t: **Assess each app with the drivers** → assign the **lightest R** that fixes its problem
sub: **Replatform** where the **database or runtime** is the pain

items: **First wave**: a **low-risk, instructive workload** with an **enthusiastic team**
**Landing zone** built in **IaC**
a.foot: Budget for the **migration bubble** before **savings** appear.

q: A team rehosted its app onto cloud VMs, but the monthly bill is higher than on premises, and the app still can't scale down at night. Diagnose this, and say what to change and what it costs.

items: **Diagnosis**: **lift and shift** carries over **over-provisioning** and the app's **inability to scale** → pays for **always-on peak capacity** on **usage-based pricing**

sub: Then **partially refactor or replatform**: make the **web tier stateless** so it can **autoscale**
Move the database to a **managed service**

items: **Cost**: **refactoring effort and testing**
a.foot: **Lift-and-optimise** would have avoided some of this, but would have taken **longer up front**.

q: Autoscaling fixes high CPU on a shop's web tier, but carts still disappear when instances are replaced and order retries create duplicate orders. Which design decisions remain, and which 12-factor principles do they relate to?

items: **Session and cart state** out of replaceable instances, in a **durable shared store** (**stateless processes**, **backing services**)
**Order writes**: protect with the required **transaction rules**; make retryable operations **idempotent**, e.g. with a **stable order identifier**
**Fast start and graceful stop** so **scale-in** doesn't drop **in-flight work** (**disposability**)
a.foot: **Scaling compute solves capacity**, not **state management or correctness**.

q: A transfer commits successfully, but a read replica briefly shows the old balance, and the customer calls support. Has ACID failed? Decide which reads must be served from where.

a.lead: **No.** The authoritative transaction **committed atomically**; **asynchronous replication is lagging**.
items: **From the primary** (or require **read-your-writes**): **balance checks right after a transfer**, and anything used for **further transfers**
**From replicas**: **statements, analytics and activity feeds**, which tolerate **staleness**
a.foot: Specify the **freshness each operation needs** rather than **one policy for the whole app**.

q: A product team plans a relational database for orders, a document store for the catalogue, a key-value cache for sessions, a graph store for recommendations and object storage for images, all for an MVP with 3 developers. Evaluate the plan against the 12 factors and the cost of polyglot persistence.

a.lead: Each choice matches an **access pattern**, but **polyglot persistence** adds **programming and operational cost** for every store, which a **3-person MVP** may not afford.
items: **Keep**: **relational database** for orders (and possibly the **catalogue**), the **cache** for sessions, **object storage** for images
**Defer** the **graph store**; compute **recommendations in batch**
**12 factors**: treat every store as an **attached backing service** configured from the **environment** → adding one later doesn't need **code changes**

q: A 'microservices' system ships all 12 services in one container image, and every change needs a joint release. What would you change in its design and its Kubernetes deployment?

sub: Give each service **stable contracts** and **private data ownership**
A **versioned image** and a **Deployment per service**

a.foot: **Kubernetes replicas only run more copies** → **release coupling** must be removed in the **application design** and in each service's **own pipeline**.

q: An order platform on managed Kubernetes calls Payment, Inventory and Email synchronously. During a sale, Email slows down and checkout fails. Give the cause, a countermeasure and its drawback, and say whether a service mesh or managed messaging would help.

items: **Cause**: **synchronous calls** to a **non-critical dependency** → **blocked threads** in checkout spread Email's slowness

sub: Publish an **'order placed' event** to a **managed queue or topic** → Email processes **asynchronously**
Keep a **time-bounded synchronous call** only to **Payment**

items: **Drawback**: **eventual consistency** and the need for **idempotent consumers**

sub: A **service mesh** helps apply **timeouts and breakers uniformly**
**Managed messaging** is what **removes the dependency from the checkout path**

q: A media company runs its upload API on Kubernetes, and a teammate wants to move the thumbnail generation (bursty, a few seconds per image) to functions and the video catalogue to a managed NoSQL database. Do you agree? Explain the knock-on effects.

a.lead: **Mostly yes.** Keep the **always-on upload API on Kubernetes**.
items: **Thumbnails → functions**: **bursty, short, event-triggered** work; **scale with uploads**, **cost nothing when idle**
**Catalogue → document or key-value store**: fits its **flexible, keyed reads**

sub: Functions: **execution limits** and **cold starts**; can **overwhelm downstream stores** → writes must be **idempotent**
Managed database: moves **operations to the provider**, but adds **lock-in through its API**

q: A private support assistant uses RAG over internal documents and a managed model API. What security work remains with the company, and when would the design need an agent rather than retrieval alone?

items.t: **Security work that remains** with the company

items: **Shared responsibility**: a **managed model API** still leaves **application and data** responsibilities with the **customer**

sub: **Actions** such as **changing an order** need an **agent with tools**
Each tool with **separate authorisation, limits and validation**

q: A RAG assistant gives accurate answers using documents the requester should not be allowed to see. A manager says the design is fine because the answers are correct and the data is encrypted. Do you agree?

items: **Encryption**: the **running application can decrypt** → it leaked data the user **wasn't entitled to**
**Information-disclosure breach**
**Fix**: **filter retrieval by the requester's permissions**; apply the same checks to any **tool calls**
**Audit evidence**: keep a record of **what was retrieved for whom**

q: An event-driven serverless pipeline processes uploaded invoices: a function extracts fields with a GenAI model, another writes to a database, and failures are retried automatically. Name two security risks and two reliability risks, with a control for each.

sub: **Over-broad function roles** → give each function **least-privilege** access to **only its bucket and table**
**Sensitive invoice data sent to an external model** → **classify the data**, confirm the provider's **terms and data location**, or **self-host an open-weight model**
**Retries creating duplicate records** → **idempotent writes keyed on the invoice ID**
**Bursts of scaled-out functions overwhelming the database** → **cap concurrency** or put a **queue** in front

a.foot: Also **log and audit model calls**: **generated extractions can be wrong** and need **validation**.

q: A ticketing company must leave its data centre in 6 months. On-sale events push traffic to 30 times normal for 15 minutes, seat inventory must never be oversold, and card data falls under strict compliance rules. Outline a staged cloud design, justify the service model per component, and name two side effects to monitor after go-live.

sub: Onto **IaaS** and a **managed relational database** → meets the **6-month exit**

items.t: **Stage 2: split out the components that spike**
sub: Event catalogue and queueing for seats → **stateless containers or functions** behind an **API gateway**

items.t: **Seat inventory**: keep seat reservation **transactional (ACID)** in the **authoritative store** → never oversold
**Compliance**: **tokenise card data**; define everything in **IaC** with a clear **shared-responsibility split**

sub: **Queue depth and wait time** (users' experience during the burst)
**Database write contention** on hot events, since **scaling compute doesn't scale the inventory store**

q: A logistics firm's monolith tracks parcels for 2 million deliveries a day. The team proposes rebuilding it as 40 microservices on Kubernetes across two clouds within a year. As the cloud architect, do you agree? Propose an alternative path and justify it with the drivers and the team's capacity.

a.lead: **Not as proposed.** Diagnose the drivers first.
items: **Drivers**: if the pain is **peak scaling and slow releases**, the root cause is **architecture and agility** → **rearchitecting the hot components** fixes it at far lower risk than a **full rebuild**
**Start small**: a **modular monolith** or a few **microliths** for the parts that change or scale differently (**tracking ingest**, **customer notifications**)
**Platform**: **one managed Kubernetes** platform with **CI/CD** and **observability**
**Add a second cloud only for a concrete reason**: data, identity and managed-service dependencies **aren't portable**, and two clouds **double operating skills**
**Grow the service count** as **maturity** (DevOps, monitoring) and **team size** allow

q: A health-tech startup is building a patient app with offline symptom logging, a clinician dashboard, a GenAI assistant that answers from clinical guidelines, and a nightly analytics job. Data must stay in-country. Propose the reference architecture: front-end choice, compute per component, data stores, integration patterns and the main security controls.

sub: Designed **offline storage and sync**; **native** only if device features demand it
**Containers** for the always-on patient and clinician APIs behind an **API gateway**
**Search or vector index** of guidelines for **RAG**
**Synchronous calls** only where a user waits

q: A team reports that its 'cloud-native' platform has 99.95% availability because every component has a 99.99% SLA. The request path crosses a gateway, three services in series and a database. Evaluate the claim and propose how to reach a real 99.95%, naming the cost of each change.

a.lead: The claim holds **only in the best case**.

sub: **Shared failure modes** and the application's **own bugs** push it lower
**Provider SLAs don't add up to an application SLA**

items: **Events and caches**: remove components from the **synchronous path** (cost: **eventual consistency**)
**Spread replicas across zones** with **health probes** and **spare capacity** (cost: more running capacity)
**Timeouts and circuit breakers** so one slow service doesn't **cascade** (cost: **degraded responses**)
**Database standby** with **tested failover** (cost: **replication overhead**)
Then **measure availability end to end**
